Q14-A.text:
# Price per bottle and how it compares

## Your cost per bottle

| Item | Amount |
|---|---|
| Carton of 12 bottles | ₦30,000 |
| Transport | ₦1,200 |
| **Total cost** | **₦31,200** |
| **Cost per bottle** | ₦31,200 ÷ 12 = **₦2,600** |

## Price for 25% profit

₦2,600 × 1.25 = **₦3,250 per bottle**

That gives you ₦650 profit per bottle, or ₦7,800 per carton.

## Will you beat your competitor?

**No.** At ₦3,250 you would be **₦150 more expensive** than his ₦3,100.

If you match or undercut him, you earn less than 25%:

| Your price | Profit per bottle | Profit % |
|---|---|---|
| ₦3,250 | ₦650 | 25% (your target) |
| ₦3,100 (match him) | ₦500 | 19.2% |
| ₦3,050 (beat him by ₦50) | ₦450 | 17.3% |
| ₦3,000 | ₦400 | 15.4% |

## Can you get 25% and still beat him?

Not with your current supplier price. Even with free transport, ₦2,500 × 1.25 = ₦3,125, which is still above ₦3,100.

Buying more cartons per trip helps only a little, because it spreads the transport cost:
- 2 cartons per trip: cost ₦2,550 per bottle, so the 25% price is ₦3,188
- 3 cartons per trip: cost ₦2,533 per bottle, so the 25% price is ₦3,167

**To sell at ₦3,099 with 25% profit, you need to buy the carton for about ₦28,550 or less**, keeping transport at ₦1,200.

## Suggestions

1. **Negotiate with your supplier** for about ₦1,500 off per carton, especially if you buy several cartons at once.
2. **Or accept about 17–19% profit** and sell at ₦3,000–₦3,100 to stay competitive.
3. **Or compete on something other than price**, such as convenience, credit for regular customers, or a friendly relationship. Then ₦3,200–₦3,250 can still work if customers prefer buying from you.

*Note: this treats 25% profit as profit on your cost. If you mean 25% of the selling price, the price would need to be about ₦3,467, which is even further above your competitor.*

Q14-B.text:
# Your Price per Bottle: ₦3,250

**At 25% profit you cannot beat your competitor.** Your price would be ₦150 above his ₦3,100.

## Your True Cost

| Item | Amount |
|---|---|
| Carton of 12 bottles | ₦30,000 |
| Transport | ₦1,200 |
| **Total cost** | **₦31,200** |
| **Cost per bottle** (₦31,200 ÷ 12) | **₦2,600** |

## Price at 25% Profit

- Profit per bottle: ₦2,600 × 25% = ₦650
- **Selling price: ₦2,600 + ₦650 = ₦3,250**
- If you sell all 12: ₦39,000 in sales, **₦7,800 profit per carton**

## Comparison with Your Competitor

| Your price | vs. ₦3,100 | Profit per bottle | Profit per carton | Profit % |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ₦3,250 | ₦150 higher | ₦650 | ₦7,800 | 25.0% |
| ₦3,100 (match him) | Same | ₦500 | ₦6,000 | 19.2% |

Removing transport doesn't fix it either. Without the ₦1,200, your cost is ₦2,500 per bottle, and 25% profit gives ₦3,125, which is still above ₦3,100.

## What It Would Take to Get Both

To make 25% and still sell at ₦3,099, your cost per bottle must be ₦2,479 or less. That means your total cost per carton (oil plus transport) must be **₦29,750 or less**, which is ₦1,450 less than you pay now. Ways to get there:

## My Recommendation

- **Meanwhile:** push your supplier for ₦1,450 off per carton, or buy 2 cartons per trip and ask for ₦850 off each. Once you're there, you can sell at ₦3,099, beat him, and keep your full 25%.

Q13-C.text:
# Invoice Reminder Email (Gentle, With Late-Fee Mention)

As of today, November 17, the invoice is **17 days overdue**. A 2% monthly late fee on $1,850 is **$37 per month**.

The approach below offers to **waive the fee if they pay by a specific date**. This lets you mention the fee without charging it. It also gives the client a reason to act soon, and it makes your terms clear for next time. The email also assumes the invoice may simply have been missed, since that's often the real reason for silence.

---

## Subject Line Options

- **Quick check-in on Invoice #2041** *(recommended: friendly and clear)*
- Invoice #2041 – friendly reminder
- Following up: Invoice #2041 ($1,850)

Put the invoice number in the subject so the email is easy to find and forward to whoever handles payments.

---

## Recommended Email

> **Subject:** Quick check-in on Invoice #2041
>
> Hi [Client Name],
>
> I hope things are going well on your end!
>
> I wanted to follow up on Invoice #2041 for $1,850, which was due on October 31. I know how easily these things get buried in a busy inbox, so I've attached a copy here for convenience.
>
> Could you let me know when I can expect payment, or if there's anything on your side I can help with? If there's an issue with the invoice or you need a different arrangement, just say so. I'm happy to work something out.
>
> As a quick heads-up, my terms include a 2% monthly late fee on overdue balances. Given how much I value working with you, I'll gladly waive it as long as payment comes through by **[date, e.g., Friday, November 28]**.
>
> You can pay via [payment method / link]. If it's already on its way, please disregard this note, and thank you!
>
> Thanks so much, and I look forward to continuing our work together.
>
> Best,
> [Your Name]
> [Phone] | [Website]

---

## Why This Works

| Element | Purpose |
|---|---|
| "Easily buried in a busy inbox" | Gives them a graceful excuse, so nobody feels accused. |
| Attaching the invoice | Removes friction. If they lost it, they don't need to ask. |
| "Let me know when I can expect payment" | Asks for a reply, which addresses their silence, without demanding money outright. |
| Offering help or a different arrangement | Brings out any hidden problem, such as a billing dispute, cash flow trouble, or a wrong contact. |
| Fee framed as a waiver | Reminds them of your terms while showing goodwill. It also sets a deadline without sounding like a threat. |
| "If it's already on its way, disregard" | Saves face for both sides if payment is already in progress. |

---

## Alternative Versions

### Softer: no fee mention
Use this if the relationship is very warm, or if you'd rather save the fee for a second reminder.

> Hi [Client Name],
>
> I hope you're doing well! Just a friendly note that Invoice #2041 for $1,850 was due on October 31. I've attached a copy in case it slipped through the cracks.
>
> Would you mind letting me know when payment might be on the way? And if there's anything I can clarify, I'm happy to help.
>
> Thanks so much. Always great working with you!
>
> Best,
> [Your Name]

### Firmer second follow-up
Send this about 7–10 days later if there's still no reply.

> **Subject:** Second reminder: Invoice #2041 now past due
>
> Hi [Client Name],
>
> I'm following up on my note from [date] about Invoice #2041 for $1,850, originally due October 31. I haven't heard back and want to make sure this reached the right person.
>
> As mentioned, my terms include a 2% monthly late fee. I'd still prefer to waive it, so if payment arrives by [new date], I'll keep the balance at $1,850. After that, the fee of $37 per month will apply per our agreement.
>
> If someone else handles accounts payable, I'd appreciate it if you could point me their way. And if something's come up, please let me know. I'm open to a payment plan if that helps.
>
> Thank you,
> [Your Name]

---

## Tips Before You Hit Send

1. **Fill in a real deadline.** About 10 days out (e.g., November 28) is reasonable. Vague phrases like "soon" don't prompt action.
2. **Include a direct payment link** if you can. It's the biggest single boost to on-time payment.
3. **Check that you're emailing the right person.** Silence often means the invoice went to someone who left or who doesn't handle payments. Consider CC'ing their accounts-payable contact if you have one.
4. **Confirm your terms were stated up front.** Only enforce the late fee if it appeared on the invoice or in your contract. If it didn't, use the softer version and add the fee clause to future invoices.
5. **Send mid-morning, Tuesday through Thursday.** Emails sent then tend to get read and acted on more often.
6. **Keep a record.** Note the date you sent this so your follow-ups have a clear timeline.

## Suggested Follow-Up Timeline

- **Today:** Send the recommended email.
- **Around 7–10 days later:** Send the firmer second follow-up if there's no reply.
- **A few days after that:** A short, friendly phone call often resolves things faster than another email.
- **30+ days of silence:** Consider pausing new work until the balance is settled, and then apply the late fee per your terms.

If you'd like, I can adjust the tone to match how you usually talk with this client (more casual, more formal, first-name basis, etc.) or tailor it to your industry.

Q14-C.text:
# Pricing Your Groundnut Oil

## Short answer

To make **at least 25% profit**, sell each bottle for **₦3,250**. That is **₦150 more than your competitor's ₦3,100**, so at that target you **will not beat him on price**.

---

## Step 1: Your true cost per bottle

Transport is part of your cost, so include it.

| Item | Amount |
|---|---|
| Carton of 12 bottles | ₦30,000 |
| Transport | ₦1,200 |
| **Total cost** | **₦31,200** |
| **Cost per bottle** (₦31,200 ÷ 12) | **₦2,600** |

If you ignored transport, you would think each bottle costs ₦2,500. Your real profit would then be lower than you think.

## Step 2: Price for 25% profit

25% profit on cost per bottle is ₦2,600 × 0.25 = **₦650**.

**Selling price = ₦2,600 + ₦650 = ₦3,250 per bottle**

Check:
- Revenue: 12 × ₦3,250 = ₦39,000
- Profit: ₦39,000 − ₦31,200 = **₦7,800 per carton**
- ₦7,800 ÷ ₦31,200 = **25%** ✅

> **Note:** Some people mean "25% profit" as 25% of the *selling price* (margin), not 25% of cost. In that case the price would be ₦2,600 ÷ 0.75 = **₦3,467**, which is even further above the competitor. This answer uses the more common meaning, 25% on cost.

## Step 3: Compare with the competitor

| Your price | Profit per bottle | Profit per carton | Profit % on cost | vs. Competitor (₦3,100) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ₦3,250 | ₦650 | ₦7,800 | **25.0%** | ₦150 more expensive ❌ |
| ₦3,100 (match) | ₦500 | ₦6,000 | 19.2% | Same price |
| ₦3,050 | ₦450 | ₦5,400 | 17.3% | ₦50 cheaper ✅ |
| ₦3,000 | ₦400 | ₦4,800 | 15.4% | ₦100 cheaper ✅ |
| ₦2,600 | ₦0 | ₦0 | 0% | Break-even, never go below this |

**You cannot get 25% profit and also be cheaper than ₦3,100 at your current costs.** The most you can make while matching him is about 19%.

---

## Step 4: How to get 25% *and* beat ₦3,100

To sell at ₦3,099 or less with 25% profit, your cost per bottle must be at most ₦3,099 ÷ 1.25 ≈ **₦2,479**. That is about ₦121 lower than your current ₦2,600.

### Option A: Spread transport over more cartons
If you bring several cartons in one trip, transport costs less per bottle:

| Cartons per trip | Cost per bottle | Price for 25% | Beats ₦3,100? |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | ₦2,600 | ₦3,250 | ❌ |
| 2 | ₦2,550 | ₦3,188 | ❌ |
| 3 | ₦2,533 | ₦3,167 | ❌ |
| 5 | ₦2,520 | ₦3,150 | ❌ |
| Free transport | ₦2,500 | ₦3,125 | ❌ |

This helps, but **it is not enough on its own**. Even with zero transport, 25% on ₦2,500 is ₦3,125.

### Option B: Negotiate a lower carton price (the real fix)
With one carton per trip, you need the carton at **about ₦28,550 or less**, a discount of roughly **₦1,450 (about 5%)**. Ways to get it:
- Ask your supplier for a discount when you buy several cartons at once.
- Compare other wholesalers or markets.
- Buy in bulk with another trader and share transport.

Combining both works well. For example, if you buy **3 cartons at ₦29,000 each** in one trip:
- Cost per bottle: (₦87,000 + ₦1,200) ÷ 36 = **₦2,450**
- Price for 25%: **₦3,063**, which is cheaper than the competitor ✅

---

## Step 5: Practical recommendations

1. **For now, you have two choices:**
   - **Keep your 25% target:** price at **₦3,250** and compete on things other than price (see point 3).
   - **Compete on price:** sell at **₦3,050** and accept about 17% profit. That is still ₦5,400 per carton, and a lower price may help you sell faster.

2. **Think about how fast you sell, not just profit per bottle.** If ₦3,050 helps you sell a carton in 1 week instead of 3, you earn much more over a month than you would with slow sales at ₦3,250.

3. **If you price above him, give customers a reason to pay more:**
   - Be closer or more convenient for them.
   - Offer friendly service or small credit to trusted customers.
   - Give a bulk deal, such as ₦3,250 each or 2 for ₦6,300.
   - Make sure your bottles are clean, sealed, and properly measured.

4. **Watch your hidden costs.** Leakage, breakage, market levies, and storage reduce your real profit. If one bottle in a carton is lost, your cost per sellable bottle rises to ₦2,836.

5. **Never sell below ₦2,600.** At that price you lose money.

---

## Summary

- **True cost per bottle:** ₦2,600 (including transport)
- **Price for 25% profit:** **₦3,250**
- **Beat the competitor at 25%?** **No.** You would be ₦150 more expensive.
- **To beat him today:** sell at ₦3,050 for about 17% profit.
- **To beat him at 25%:** lower your cost to about ₦2,479 per bottle, mainly by negotiating the carton price down about 5% and buying several cartons per trip.

Q17-A.text:
# Thesis Plan: 17 Nov 2026 to 31 May 2027

**Key dates**
- **Mid-January:** Lab data complete
- **Friday 30 April:** Full draft to supervisor. Four weeks before the deadline is 3 May. Aiming a few days earlier protects you from slippage.
- **May:** Revisions based on feedback
- **Monday 31 May:** Submission

Because your data won't be ready until mid-January, use **November to January for everything that doesn't depend on results**. That way you won't be writing the whole thesis in February to April.

**Weekly time budget:** With 15 h/week of work, plan for about **20–25 h/week on the thesis** (lab plus writing). Protect 2–3 fixed writing blocks per week, ideally mornings.

## Late November (17–30 Nov): Setup and structure
- Meet your supervisor to agree on the **chapter outline**, the expected length, and the format requirements (template, citation style, page limits).
- Set up your tools: a reference manager (Zotero or Mendeley), the thesis template, and file backups or version control.
- Draft a **detailed outline** with headings and 2–3 bullet points per section.
- Collect and organise the literature you've already read.
- **Goal:** Approved outline and a working document.

## December: Literature review and methods
- Write the **literature review / theoretical background**. Target a solid first draft by about 20 Dec.
- Write the **methods chapter**. You already know your experimental setup, sampling, and analytical procedures, so this can be written now.
- Plan your **data analysis** (statistics, software, scripts). If possible, build scripts with your partial data.
- Holidays: plan for little or no work from about 23 Dec to 1 Jan. Treat it as rest, not as catch-up time.
- **Goal:** First drafts of the literature review and methods (roughly 30–40% of the thesis text).

## January: Finish lab work and start analysis
- **1–15 Jan:** Lab work has priority. In the evenings, do light tasks such as revising the methods and fixing references.
- **Mid–late Jan:** Clean, organise, and quality-check all data. Run the analyses and make **first versions of figures and tables**.
- Send the supervisor your lit review and methods drafts for **early informal feedback**, if they're willing. This is much cheaper than finding problems in May.
- **Goal:** All data processed, with preliminary figures and tables.

## February: Results
- Finalise your figures and tables. Decide which ones go in the main text and which go in the appendix.
- Write the **results chapter**: describe what you found, without interpreting it yet.
- Hold a short meeting with your supervisor to discuss key findings and agree on the story of the thesis.
- **Goal:** Complete results draft.

## March: Discussion
- Write the **discussion**: interpret the results, compare them with the literature, and cover limitations and implications for environmental practice.
- This is usually the hardest chapter, so give it the whole month.
- Update the literature review if your results point to new relevant work.
- **Goal:** Complete discussion draft.

## April: Complete and polish the draft
- **1–15 Apr:** Write the **introduction** (objectives and research questions), the **conclusion**, and the **abstract**. These are easier once you know the full story.
- **15–28 Apr:** Do a full read-through for consistency between chapters, and check figure numbering, references, units, and formatting.
- **30 Apr:** Send the full draft to your supervisor.
- **Goal:** Complete draft submitted.

## May: Revision and submission
- **1–15 May (waiting for feedback):** Do the appendices, list of abbreviations, acknowledgements, and declaration forms. Proofread, or ask a friend to.
- **When feedback arrives:** Prioritise the content and structure comments first, then the minor ones.
- **By about 24 May:** Finish revisions. Run a final format check and plagiarism check if one is required.
- **By 28 May:** Print and bind if needed (check the print shop's lead time), then submit early. Don't count on 31 May going smoothly.

## Tips
- **Agree on this timeline with your supervisor** now, including when they'll return feedback in May.
- **Tell your employer** early that late April and May will be busy. Ask whether you can reduce or shift hours then.
- **Track progress weekly** (for example, word count or sections finished each Friday). If a month slips, you'll notice quickly.
- **Buffer:** If something goes wrong, such as lab delays or failed analyses, the December holiday period and the second half of April are your main fallback slots.

Q12-A.text:
# Half Marathon Plan: 16 Weeks to March 8

**Your race falls on a Monday.** March 8, 2027 is a Monday, the first day of your shift block. The race itself fits, since you'd be off Sunday night and racing in the morning. But a 12-hour night shift right after a half marathon will be rough. If you can, book Monday night off now. If you can't, plan for a long nap after the race.

## How the week works

| Day | Session | Timing |
|---|---|---|
| **Thu** | Easy run | **Evening.** You're coming off a night shift, so sleep first. |
| **Fri** | Key workout (strides, tempo, or race pace) | Early morning or evening |
| **Sat** | Rest or optional short easy run | Flexible |
| **Sun** | **Long run** | **Early morning**, finished before 7am |
| Mon–Wed | Off (work) | Light walking or stretching only if you feel like it |

**Easy** means a conversational pace, where you could talk in full sentences. Most of your running should feel like this.

## The schedule (distances in km)

| Wk | Dates | Thu (easy) | Fri (workout) | Sat | Sun (long) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Nov 19–22 | 4 | 5 easy | Rest | **8** |
| 2 | Nov 26–29 | 4 | 5 easy + 4×20s strides | Rest | **9** |
| 3 | Dec 3–6 | 5 | 6 incl. 6×1 min brisk / 2 min easy | Rest | **10** |
| 4 | Dec 10–13 | 4 | 5 easy + strides | Rest | **8** (cutback) |
| 5 | Dec 17–20 | 5 | 6 incl. 3×5 min tempo | 3 optional | **11** |
| 6 | Dec 24–27 | 5 | 6 easy (holiday, so stay flexible) | Rest | **12** |
| 7 | Dec 31–Jan 3 | 5 | 7 incl. 2×8 min tempo | 3 optional | **13** |
| 8 | Jan 7–10 | 5 | 6 easy + strides | Rest | **10** (cutback) |
| 9 | Jan 14–17 | 6 | 7 incl. 3×8 min tempo | 4 optional | **14** |
| 10 | Jan 21–24 | 6 | 8 incl. 5×3 min hard / 2 min jog | 4 optional | **15** |
| 11 | Jan 28–31 | 6 | 8 incl. 20 min tempo | 4 optional | **16** |
| 12 | Feb 4–7 | 5 | 6 easy + strides | Rest | **12** (cutback) |
| 13 | Feb 11–14 | 6 | 8 incl. 2×12 min tempo | 4 optional | **17** |
| 14 | Feb 18–21 | 6 | 9 incl. 25 min at goal race pace | 4 optional | **18** (peak) |
| 15 | Feb 25–28 | 5 | 7 incl. 15 min at race pace | 3 optional | **13** (taper) |
| 16 | Mar 4–7 | 4 | 5 easy + 4 strides | Rest | Rest or 3 km shakeout |
| | **Mon Mar 8** | | | | 🏁 **21.1 km** |

- **Tempo** means "comfortably hard." You can speak a few words, not full sentences.
- **Strides** are 20-second smooth, quick pickups with full recovery between them. Do them at the end of the run.
- Every workout includes about 1–2 km of easy jogging to warm up and cool down. This is counted in the total.

## Things specific to your situation

**Shift recovery comes first.** Thursday is the day you're most likely to be wrecked. If you slept badly, skip Thursday or cut it to 20 minutes. Never skip Sunday's long run to make up for a missed Thursday.

**Heat:**
- From week 9 on, long runs take 1.5–2 hours, so start them by about 5:00–5:15am to finish before 7.
- Carry water on anything over 10 km. Add electrolytes once runs pass about 75 minutes.
- Practice your race-day food and drink on long runs. Nothing new on race day.

**Check the race start time.** Do a couple of your later long runs at that same time of day so your body is used to it.

**Missed a week?** Repeat it rather than jumping ahead. You have a little slack built in.

**Warning signs:** Sharp or localized pain, or pain that changes how you run, means rest a few days. Don't push through it.

Q19-A.text:
**Q4 Sales Summary**

Our team of five closed KES 9.6 million against a quarterly target of KES 12 million, reaching **80%** of target. The KES 2.4 million gap is mostly explained by two large deals worth a combined KES 2.1 million, which slipped into January. Had these closed within the quarter, we would have reached KES 11.7 million, or **97.5%** of target. Both deals remain active, and we expect them to give us a strong start to Q1.

**The math:**
- 9.6 ÷ 12 = 80%
- (9.6 + 2.1) ÷ 12 = 11.7 ÷ 12 = 97.5%
- Remaining gap even with the slipped deals: KES 0.3 million (2.5%)

**Tips for Friday:**
- **Be ready for "why did they slip?"** A brief reason (client budget cycle, procurement delays, legal review) makes the explanation more credible.
- **Give January close dates if you can.** Something like "both are expected to sign by mid-January" turns the slip into a concrete forecast.
- **Mention the remaining 2.5%.** It shows you aren't relying only on the slipped deals to explain the miss.

Q17-B.text:
# Thesis Plan: 17 November 2026 to 31 May 2027

## Key dates

| Date | Milestone |
|---|---|
| **Fri 15 Jan 2027** | Lab data collection finished |
| **Fri 30 Apr 2027** | Full draft sent to supervisor (target) |
| **Mon 3 May 2027** | Latest possible draft date (4 weeks before deadline) |
| **Fri 28 May 2027** | Final version complete |
| **Mon 31 May 2027** | Submission deadline |

You have about 28 weeks. The plan sends the draft on Friday 30 April. That leaves the weekend as a small buffer before the 3 May cutoff. It also has you finishing on 28 May, so a printing or upload problem won't cost you the deadline.

**Weekly time budget:** Your student assistant job takes 15 hours. If you treat the thesis and job together as a 40–45 hour week, you have about **25–30 thesis hours per week**. Until mid-January, most of that goes to the lab, so writing gets about **6–8 hours a week**. From mid-January onward, writing and analysis get nearly all of it.

**The main principle:** Don't wait for the data before you start writing. The literature review and methods chapters don't depend on your results, so you can draft them now.

---

## November (17–30 Nov): Set up

- **Outline the thesis** chapter by chapter: Introduction, Literature Review, Methods, Results, Discussion, Conclusions. Under each heading, write 3–5 bullet points on what it will cover.
- **Book a meeting with your supervisor** before the end of November. At the meeting:
  - agree on the outline;
  - confirm 30 April as your draft date;
  - ask whether they'll look at single chapters before then (planned below for February and March);
  - ask how long they usually need for feedback.
- **Set up your tools:**
  - a reference manager (Zotero or Mendeley) with your existing sources loaded;
  - the university thesis template;
  - one folder system for drafts, data, and figures.
- **Fix two writing blocks per week** of 3–4 hours each, at times that don't clash with your work shifts or lab sessions.
- **Start a methods log.** After each lab session, write down the procedures, equipment, settings, sample IDs, and any deviations. This becomes your methods chapter almost word for word.

## December: Literature review and methods

- **Draft the literature review.** Aim for a complete rough version by Fri 18 Dec. It doesn't need to be polished.
- **Draft the methods chapter** from your log: site and sample description, experimental setup, analytical methods, QA/QC, and the statistical approach you plan to use.
- **Build your analysis pipeline now** using the data you already have. Write the scripts or spreadsheets and set up the figure templates, so January's analysis is a matter of feeding in the rest of the data.
- **Holidays (24 Dec–1 Jan):** Take this week off or keep it light. Plan for it so it doesn't become an unplanned slip.

## January: Finish the lab and start analysis

- **1–15 Jan:** Lab work comes first. Keep writing to one block a week, spent tidying the methods chapter.
- **By Fri 15 Jan:** All data collected. Do a completeness check so you don't discover a missing sample in March.
- **18–31 Jan:** Clean the data, run the full analysis, and produce draft versions of every figure and table.
- **End of January:** Write a one-page summary of your key findings. This guides the results and discussion chapters.

## February: Results chapter

- **Write the results chapter** around the figures and tables. Describe what the data show and save interpretation for the discussion.
- **Mid-February:** Send the results chapter or key figures to your supervisor for a quick check. Catching a problem in your analysis now is much cheaper than finding it in May.
- **Finalise the methods chapter** so it matches exactly what you did and analysed.
- **Target:** Results draft done by **Fri 26 Feb**.

## March: Discussion and introduction

- **Write the discussion (1–19 Mar).** Interpret your results, compare them with the studies in your literature review, cover limitations, and draw out implications for environmental engineering practice. This is the hardest chapter, so give it the most time.
- **Revise the literature review (22–26 Mar)** so it sets up your discussion. Cut sources you no longer need and add any the discussion made necessary.
- **Write the introduction (29–31 Mar):** problem statement, research questions, and thesis structure. It's easier to write once you know what the thesis actually argues.

## April: Complete the draft

- **1–9 Apr:** Write the conclusions and abstract. Check that every research question in the introduction is answered.
- **12–23 Apr:** Read the whole thesis start to finish. Fix the logic between chapters, terminology, figure numbering, cross-references, and citations.
- **26–29 Apr:** Formatting, references list, appendices (raw data, extra figures), and table of contents.
- **Fri 30 Apr:** Send the full draft to your supervisor.

## May: Feedback and submission

- **3–14 May (waiting for feedback):** Proofread, check units and significant figures, and finish front matter and acknowledgements. Check your university's submission rules: format, binding or upload method, declarations, and plagiarism check.
- **When feedback arrives (around 14–17 May):** Sort the comments into major changes (content and structure) and minor ones (wording and formatting). Do the major changes first.
- **17–26 May:** Revise. This is your heaviest thesis period, so tell your employer early and try to reduce or rearrange your 15 hours for these two weeks.
- **27–28 May:** Final read-through, PDF export, and printing or upload checks.
- **Fri 28 May:** Submit, three days ahead of the 31 May deadline.

---

## Checkpoints

If you miss any of these by more than a week, adjust the plan right away:

1. **Fri 18 Dec:** Literature review rough draft done.

# Saturday Tournament Rotation Plan

## Can everyone get exactly equal minutes?

Not quite, because only Tunde and Chidi can play in goal.

- **Total time:** 4 matches × 30 min = **120 minutes**, and someone must be in goal for all of it.
- **Keepers:** If they split goal evenly, each plays at least **60 minutes**.
- **Outfield:** 16 players share 6 spots × 120 min = 720 minutes, which is **45 minutes each**.

So the fairest result is **keepers 60 minutes, everyone else 45 minutes.** Nobody gets fewer than 45.

## Goalkeepers

| Match | In goal | Other keeper |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Tunde | Rests |
| 2 | Chidi | Rests |
| 3 | Tunde | Rests |
| 4 | Chidi | Rests |

## Outfield rotation (16 players, labelled A–P)

Each half is split at the 7:30 mark, so every match has **4 blocks of 7.5 minutes**. Each block uses a full line change of 6 players.

| Block | Match 1 & Match 3 | Match 2 & Match 4 |
|---|---|---|
| 1st half, 0:00–7:30 | A B C D E F | I J K L M N |
| 1st half, 7:30–15:00 | G H I J K L | O P A B C D |
| 2nd half, 0:00–7:30 | M N O P A B | E F G H I J |
| 2nd half, 7:30–15:00 | C D E F G H | K L M N O P |

**How it works out:**
- Every outfield player plays **6 blocks = 45 minutes**.
- Every child plays in **all 4 matches**:
  - A–H play 15 minutes in Matches 1 and 3, and 7.5 minutes in Matches 2 and 4.
  - I–P play the reverse.
- **Nobody plays two blocks in a row**, so everyone gets a rest after each stint.
- Matches 3 and 4 repeat Matches 1 and 2, so you only need to remember two match sheets.

## Tips

1. **Mixing the groups:** Spread strong and less experienced players across A–P so every line is balanced. Pair defenders and attackers so each block has a sensible shape.
2. **Fewer swaps:** If a 6-player change is chaotic, roll the subs in over a minute or two at the 7:30 mark.
3. **Using the resting keeper:** You could put the resting keeper in an outfield block or two, but that pushes their total further above everyone else's.
4. **Injuries or no-shows:** If someone can't play, the plan still works with 15 outfielders at 48 minutes each. Let me know and I'll rework it.

# Half Marathon Plan: Thu–Sun Training, Race Monday March 8, 2027

**Before you start: March 8, 2027 is a Monday,** which is the first night of your shift week. If you race that morning and then work a 12-hour night shift, the shift will be rough and your recovery will suffer. Ask now to have Monday night off or swapped. The plan below keeps Sunday March 7 nearly empty so you arrive at the race fresh.

**Timeline:** The plan runs 16 weeks, from Thursday Nov 19, 2026 to the race on Mon Mar 8, 2027. Your long run builds from 8 km to a peak of 18 km three weeks before the race.

## Weekly structure

| Day | What | When |
|---|---|---|
| Mon–Wed | No running (night shifts) | — |
| **Thu** | Easy run | **Evening** (~6:00 pm), after your post-shift sleep. Don't run straight off the shift. |
| **Fri** | Workout | **Evening** (~6:00 pm), while your body clock is still shifting back |
| **Sat** | Rest | Separates the workout from the long run |
| **Sun** | Long run | **Early morning**, finished before 7:00 am |

**Sunday start times** assume an easy pace of about 7:00 per km plus a 10-minute buffer. Once you know your real long-run pace, adjust them. If Sunday mornings are ever impossible, Sunday evening is the backup.

## The 16-week plan

| Wk | Dates | Thu (easy) | Fri (workout) | Sun (long) | Sun start by | Week total |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Nov 19–22 | 4 km | 5 km easy + 4 strides | 8 km | 5:50 am | 17 km |
| 2 | Nov 26–29 | 4 km | 5 km easy + 6 strides | 9 km | 5:45 am | 18 km |
| 3 | Dec 3–6 | 5 km | **A** (6 km) | 10 km | 5:40 am | 21 km |
| 4 | Dec 10–13 | 4 km | 5 km easy + 4 strides | 8 km *(cutback)* | 5:50 am | 17 km |
| 5 | Dec 17–20 | 5 km | **B** (7 km) | 11 km | 5:30 am | 23 km |
| 6 | Dec 24–27 | 5 km | **C** (7 km) | 12 km | 5:25 am | 24 km |
| 7 | Dec 31–Jan 3 | 4 km | 6 km easy + 6 strides | 10 km *(cutback)* | 5:40 am | 20 km |
| 8 | Jan 7–10 | 6 km | **D** (8 km) | 13 km | 5:15 am | 27 km |
| 9 | Jan 14–17 | 6 km | **E** (8 km) | 14 km | 5:10 am | 28 km |
| 10 | Jan 21–24 | 5 km | 6 km easy + 6 strides | 11 km *(cutback)* | 5:30 am | 22 km |
| 11 | Jan 28–31 | 6 km | **F** (9 km) | 15 km | 5:05 am | 30 km |
| 12 | Feb 4–7 | 7 km | **G** (9 km) | 16 km | 4:55 am | 32 km |
| 13 | Feb 11–14 | 5 km | 7 km easy + 6 strides | 13 km *(cutback)* | 5:15 am | 25 km |
| 14 | Feb 18–21 | 7 km | **H** (10 km) | **18 km (peak)** | 4:40 am | 35 km |
| 15 | Feb 25–28 | 6 km | **I** (8 km) | 13 km | 5:15 am | 27 km |
| 16 | Mar 4–7 | 5 km + 4 strides | **J** (5 km) | 15-min shakeout or rest | 6:00 am | ~12 km |
| **Race** | **Mon Mar 8** | | | **21.1 km** | | |

## Effort guide

You haven't raced these distances yet, so the plan uses effort instead of pace:

- **Easy:** You can talk in full sentences. Most of your running is at this effort, including every Thursday and Sunday run.
- **Strides:** 20 seconds of fast, relaxed running, then walk or jog until you've recovered.
- **Half-marathon (HM) effort:** Comfortably hard. You can only manage a few words at a time, and it feels sustainable for a long time.
- **Tempo:** A bit harder than HM effort. You could hold it for about an hour in a race.
- **10K effort:** Hard, but controlled.

## Friday workouts

Every workout includes its warm-up and cool-down in the distance shown.

- **A (6 km):** 1.5 km easy, then 6 × (1 min moderately hard / 2 min easy jog), then 1.5 km easy.
- **B (7 km):** 2 km easy, then 3 × 5 min tempo with 2 min jog between, then 1.5 km easy.
- **C (7 km):** 2 km easy, then 5 × 3 min at 10K effort with 2 min jog between, then 1.5 km easy.
- **D (8 km):** 2 km easy, then 2 × 10 min tempo with 3 min jog between, then 1.5 km easy.
- **E (8 km):** 1.5 km easy, then 6 × 800 m at 10K effort with 400 m jog between, then 1.5 km easy.
- **F (9 km):** 2 km easy, then 20 min continuous tempo, then 2 km easy.
- **G (9 km):** 2 km easy, then 5 km at HM effort, then 2 km easy.
- **H (10 km):** 2 km easy, then 3 × 2 km at HM effort with 2 min jog between, then 1.5 km easy.
- **I (8 km):** 2 km easy, then 4 km at HM effort, then 2 km easy.
- **J (5 km):** 2 km easy, then 2 km at HM effort, then 1 km easy. This is the race-week sharpener.

## Rules that make this work

1. **Never move a missed run into Mon–Wed.** If you miss one, skip it. If you miss a Sunday long run, repeat that week's long run the following Sunday instead of jumping ahead.
2. **The Thursday run is optional if you slept badly after Wednesday's shift.** Sleep matters more than 4–7 easy kilometres.
3. **Hydration and heat:** Drink 400–500 ml of water before every Sunday long run. From Week 8 onward (13 km and up), carry water. From Week 11 onward (15 km and up), take a gel or similar fuel every 40–45 minutes. Practice the exact fuel you'll use on race day.
4. **Running in the dark:** Your 4:40–5:30 am starts will be in darkness, so wear a headlamp and reflective gear.
5. **Pain rule:** Sharp pain or pain that changes how you run means stop that run. If it's still there on Thursday, take the whole week off.

## Race week and race day

- **Sat Mar 6:** Rest. Eat normal, carb-forward meals and drink well.
- **Sun Mar 7:** Either a 15-minute easy shakeout at 6:00 am or full rest. Lay out your gear, go to bed early, and keep your normal day schedule.
- **Mon Mar 8 (race):**
  - Eat a familiar breakfast 2.5–3 hours before the start.
  - Run the first 5 km slightly slower than HM effort and settle in from there.
  - Take fuel every 40–45 minutes, just as you practised.
  - Drink at every water station, since it gets hot after 7:00 am.
  - Afterward, eat and rest. Ideally you won't be working that night.

Q16-A.text:
# 12-Day Portugal Itinerary: Lisbon, Alentejo & Algarve (May 2027)

## Why this route

Lisbon and Porto are both very hilly. I've left Porto out and paired Lisbon with **Évora** (gentle slopes) and the **Algarve** (flat waterfront towns and boat trips). Those places put the sightseeing on boats, trains and promenades rather than steep climbs.

The plan uses taxis and rideshare in Lisbon, then a **rental car for days 5–11**. The car means door-to-door travel with no hauling luggage up cobbled hills.

## Day-by-Day

**Day 1 – Arrive Lisbon**
- Overnight flight from Columbus. There's no nonstop, so you'll connect via Newark, JFK, Boston, Philadelphia or Toronto.
- Stay in **Baixa or Avenida da Liberdade**. They're the flattest central areas.
- Easy, flat stroll from Rua Augusta to Praça do Comércio on the river. Early dinner and rest.

**Day 2 – Belém (completely flat)**
- Uber (~€8) or Tram 15 to Belém.
- Jerónimos Monastery, then custard tarts at Pastéis de Belém.
- Riverside walk to the Discoveries Monument and Belém Tower. Benches are plentiful.
- Evening: Time Out Market, which has lots of seating.

**Day 3 – Castle, Alfama & Fado**
- Taxi or tuk-tuk to the **Castelo de São Jorge** gate rather than walking up.
- Take another tuk-tuk to the Portas do Sol viewpoint.
- Afternoon: the **Gulbenkian Museum** and gardens, which are flat and peaceful.
- Evening: fado dinner. Book a place your taxi can drop you near.
- *Knee note:* Alfama's steep downhill stretches can be harder on knees than going up, so ride both ways if needed.

**Day 4 – Sintra day trip**
- Train from Rossio station (~40 min, ~€2.50).
- Take bus 434 or a tuk-tuk to **Pena Palace**. Buy the park shuttle from the entrance up to the palace, because that climb is steep.
- Skip the Moorish Castle (very steep). Quinta da Regaleira is optional; it has many stairs.
- Back to Lisbon by late afternoon to rest.

**Day 5 – Drive to Évora (~1.5 hrs)**
- Pick up the rental car and ask for a Via Verde toll transponder.
- Afternoon in Évora: Roman Temple, the Cathedral, and the Chapel of Bones.
- Book a hotel with parking just inside or outside the town walls.

**Day 6 – Alentejo wine & countryside**
- Morning: the **Almendres Cromlech** megaliths. It's a short, mostly level dirt path.
- Afternoon: winery visit and lunch. Cartuxa is in Évora; Herdade do Esporão is ~40 min away.
- Optional: the hilltop village of **Monsaraz**. You can park right by the gate, and the village is small.

**Day 7 – Drive to Tavira (~2.5 hrs)**
- Tavira is one of the flattest, prettiest Algarve towns, with a riverside and a Roman bridge.
- Relaxed evening and seafood dinner.

**Day 8 – Ria Formosa lagoon**
- Boat tour of the Ria Formosa lagoon (~2–3 hrs, birds and islands).
- Or take the little train from Pedras d'El Rei to **Praia do Barril** beach, which saves a long sand walk.

**Day 9 – Benagil caves → Lagos (~1.5 hrs total driving)**
- Take a Benagil cave boat tour from **Portimão marina**. Boarding from the dock is far easier than from the beach.
- Continue to Lagos and check in.

**Day 10 – Lagos**
- Boat trip to the **Ponta da Piedade** grottos. Small boats get right into the rock formations, which avoids the long cliff stairs.
- Flat marina and waterfront strolling.
- Optional drive to **Cabo de São Vicente** at sunset. You can park right by the lighthouse.

**Day 11 – Back to Lisbon (~3 hrs)**
- Return the car at the airport.
- Stay in **Parque das Nações**. It's flat, modern, on the river, and 10 min from the airport.
- Visit the Oceanário, ride the riverside cable car, and have a farewell dinner.

**Day 12 – Fly home**

## Rough Budget (for two, USD)

| Category | Estimate | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Flights CMH–LIS round trip | $2,300 | ~$1,050–1,300 pp; biggest variable |
| Lodging (11 nights) | $1,400 | Lisbon 5 nights ~$140, Évora 2 ~$110, Algarve 4 ~$120 |
| Food & drink | $1,000 | ~$85/day; Portugal is very affordable |
| Car rental (6 days), fuel, tolls, parking | $500 | Book early; automatics cost more and sell out |
| Lisbon taxis, Uber, trains | $120 | Rideshare is cheap (€5–10 per ride) |
| Sights & tours | $400 | Palaces, boat trips, wine tasting, fado |
| Travel insurance | $180 | Worth it |
| **Total** | **~$5,900** | ~$100 buffer |

**This budget is tight**, and flights are the deciding factor. If you need more room:
- Drop the car and use trains and buses. This saves ~$300 but means more walking with luggage.
- Spend a 5th night in Tavira instead of moving to Lagos, and do Benagil as a day trip.
- Eat your main meal at lunch. The *prato do dia* (dish of the day) is often €10–14 with a drink.

## Knee-Friendly Tips
- **Ask every hotel about an elevator.** Many older Lisbon buildings don't have one.
- Portugal's limestone sidewalks (*calçada*) are slippery and uneven. Wear supportive, grippy shoes and consider a folding cane or trekking pole.
- Lisbon's Elevador da Glória and Santa Justa are slow and touristy. A €5 Uber is usually the better choice.
- Plan one main activity per day with an afternoon rest. I've kept the pace light for this reason.

## Booking Checklist
- **Flights:** set fare alerts now and book by January–February. TAP, United and Delta all work with one stop.
- **Car:** reserve an automatic early.
- **Fado and Pena Palace:** book tickets in advance.
- **ETIAS:** check whether the EU's new travel authorization is in effect before you go. If so, it's a small online fee.
- **Driving:** an International Driving Permit from AAA (~$20) is recommended.

Would you like me to swap in Porto or the Douro Valley, or adjust the hotel level up or down?

# Quarterly Summary for the Regional Director

## The Numbers

| Metric | Amount (KES) | % of Target |
|---|---|---|
| Quarterly target | 12,000,000 | 100% |
| Closed this quarter | 9,600,000 | **80.0%** |
| Slipped deals (2) | 2,100,000 | 17.5% |
| Closed + slipped | 11,700,000 | **97.5%** |
| Remaining gap even with slipped deals | 300,000 | 2.5% |

How these were calculated:
- 9.6M ÷ 12M = **80%**
- (9.6M + 2.1M) ÷ 12M = 11.7M ÷ 12M = **97.5%**
- Shortfall against target: 12M − 9.6M = **2.4M**. The slipped deals account for 2.1M of that, which is about **87.5% of the gap**.

## Draft Summary Paragraph

> **Q[X] Performance Summary:** The team closed KES 9.6 million against a quarterly target of KES 12 million, achieving 80% of target. The shortfall is largely a timing issue. Two significant deals with a combined value of KES 2.1 million have moved into January. Had they closed within the quarter, the team would have reached KES 11.7 million, or 97.5% of target. These two deals account for nearly 90% of the KES 2.4 million gap. Both remain active, and we expect them to close in January, which should give the team a strong start to the new period.

## Alternative Version (more direct, if your director prefers brevity)

> The team delivered KES 9.6M against a KES 12M target (80%). Two deals worth KES 2.1M combined slipped into January. Including them, we would have reached 97.5% of target. We are tracking both closely for early-January closure.

## Tips Before You Send

1. **Own the 80% figure.** Lead with the actual result rather than the adjusted one. Directors usually trust a report more when the real number comes first and the context follows.
2. **Expect a question about the remaining KES 300K.** Even with the slipped deals you would be 2.5% short. Have a one-line explanation ready.
3. **Add confidence evidence if you have it.** Signed LOIs, approved POs, or confirmed January dates make the "timing issue" claim much stronger. For example: *"Both clients have confirmed budget approval and we have closing meetings scheduled for the week of January 12."*
4. **Say why they slipped**, briefly: client procurement delays, budget cycles, holiday timing, and so on. This shows you understand the cause and aren't just hoping.
5. **Consider a lesson or action.** One sentence such as *"We are tightening close-date forecasting on large deals"* shows proactive management.
6. **Fill in the quarter label** (Q[X]) and make sure the period matches your company's fiscal calendar.

I can also turn this into an email with a subject line, or add a short per-rep breakdown if you have the individual numbers.

# Saturday Rotation: 18 Players, 4 Matches, 7-a-side

## The numbers

- Total match time: 4 matches × 30 min = **120 minutes**
- Total playing time to share: 120 × 7 = **840 player-minutes**
- Goal must be covered for all 120 minutes by Tunde and Chidi alone, so they split it **60 / 60**.
- That leaves 6 outfield spots × 120 min = 720 minutes for the other 16 kids, which is **45 minutes each**.

This is the fairest split possible. Tunde and Chidi have to cover 120 goalkeeping minutes between them, so at least one of them would get 60 or more whatever you do. Giving each exactly 60 keeps everyone as close as the goalkeeping requirement allows.

**Subs happen only at half-time.** Nobody comes off mid-half, so there's nothing to track during play.

## Your other 16 players

You haven't told me their names, so I've numbered them 1–16. Write a name next to each number once. They're arranged in pairs that always play together, so put two kids who suit each other in each pair, ideally one more defensive and one more attacking. Spread your strongest players across different pairs.

## Match-by-match lineup

| Match | Half | Goal | Outfield (6) | Resting |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **1** | 1st | Tunde | 5, 6, 9, 10, 13, 14 | Chidi, 1–4, 7, 8, 11, 12, 15, 16 |

| **4** | 1st | Chidi | 1, 2, 7, 8, 9, 10 | Tunde, 3–6, 11–16 |

## Minutes per player

| Player(s) | Halves played | Minutes | Match fully off |
|---|---|---|---|
| Tunde | M1 1st, M2 2nd, M3 1st, M4 2nd (in goal) | **60** | none |
| Chidi | M1 2nd, M2 1st, M3 2nd, M4 1st (in goal) | **60** | none |
| 1, 2 | M2 1st, M3 2nd, M4 1st | **45** | Match 1 |
| 3, 4 | M2 2nd, M3 1st, M4 2nd | **45** | Match 1 |
| 5, 6 | M1 1st, M3 2nd, M4 2nd | **45** | Match 2 |
| 7, 8 | M1 2nd, M3 1st, M4 1st | **45** | Match 2 |

## Why it's fair

- Every outfield child plays **3 halves in 3 different matches** and never plays both halves of the same match, so they're always fresh.
- Every outfield child sits out **exactly one** match. Four pairs sit out each match, and it rotates.
- Tunde and Chidi each **start in goal twice** and alternate every half, so neither keeps goal two halves in a row.
- Every half has exactly 1 keeper and 6 outfield players, making 7 on the pitch.

## If something goes wrong

- **A child gets injured or is too tired:** bring on the resting player from the same pair, or else anyone who has played the fewest halves so far.
- **You need an emergency outfield player:** whichever of Tunde or Chidi is not in goal that half can step in.
- **Someone doesn't turn up:** their partner's halves stay the same. Fill the missing child's 3 halves with three different resting kids so the extra time is spread out.

Q20-C.text:
# Customer Apology Reply: Late Birthday Bouquet

## The main reply (email or longer message)

> Hi [Name],
>
> I'm really sorry your bouquet arrived late yesterday. I know timing matters most on a birthday, and it wasn't the experience we wanted for you.
>
> Our driver had a flat tyre on the way, which held up deliveries for about two hours. That's the reason, but I know it doesn't change how it felt on the day.
>
> To make up for it, I'd like to offer you a choice:
>
> - **A $20 refund** to your original payment method, or
> - **A free small posy** with your next order, whenever you'd like it.
>
> Just reply and let me know which you'd prefer, and I'll sort it out straight away.
>
> Thank you for letting us know, and I hope the birthday itself was a lovely one.
>
> Warm regards,
> [Your name]
> [Shop name]

## Why it's written this way

**Apologetic but not grovelling**
- It apologises once, clearly, at the start. Repeating "so sorry" several times starts to sound anxious rather than sincere.
- It doesn't use phrases like "we've completely failed you" or "this is unacceptable." The situation doesn't call for that, and over-apologising can make a small problem feel bigger.

**The flat tyre is mentioned, not used as an excuse**
- Giving the real reason helps. It shows this was a one-off, not carelessness.
- The next line, "it doesn't change how it felt on the day," stops it sounding like you're blaming the tyre to avoid responsibility. You can say it wasn't your fault without saying it.
- It skips "unforeseen circumstances beyond our control." That's the corporate version, and angry customers tend to read it as deflection.

**It acknowledges what upset her**
- The upset isn't really about two hours. It's that it was a birthday. Naming that shows you understand.
- It doesn't mention her being angry. Saying "I understand you're upset" can feel patronising. Responding to the problem is enough.

**Why I'd let her choose**
- She's been inconvenienced, so letting her pick gives back a bit of control.
- You stay within your limit of one or the other.
- Her choice also tells you something. If she takes the refund, she may not return. If she takes the posy, she probably will.
- If you'd rather not ask (some people find choices tiring when they're annoyed), see the alternative below.

**The ending**
- "I hope the birthday itself was a lovely one" closes on her and the occasion rather than on the problem. It's warm without being overdone.

## Alternative: offer one thing only

If you'd rather decide for her, replace the choice section with one of these:

**Refund (best if she seemed very annoyed or is a one-time customer):**
> To make up for it, I've refunded $20 to your original payment method. You should see it within [X] working days.

**Posy (best if she's a regular or the tone was more disappointed than furious):**
> To make up for it, I'd love to include a free small posy with your next order. Just mention this message when you order and we'll add it in.

Doing it straight away ("I've refunded") feels more generous than asking her to reply. That's worth considering if you think she won't bother writing back.

## Shorter version (text or social media)

> Hi [Name], I'm really sorry your bouquet arrived late. I know that matters most on a birthday. Our driver had a flat tyre on the way, which held everything up by about two hours. I'd like to make it up to you with either a $20 refund or a free small posy on your next order. Just let me know which you'd prefer! [Your name]

## Before you send

1. **Check the flowers arrived in good condition.** If they sat in a van for an extra two hours, they might have wilted. If she mentioned that, add a line such as "and if the flowers weren't at their best because of the delay, please let me know."
2. **Check whether she was the buyer or the recipient.** If someone else ordered them for her, the refund should go to the buyer's payment method. In that case the posy is probably the better offer, since she can actually use it.
3. **Reply soon.** A quick, calm reply today will help more than perfect wording tomorrow.
4. **If she replies still angry,** don't add a second offer. Thank her, restate the apology once, and keep the original offer open. You've been fair.

## Things to avoid adding

- "Unfortunately these things happen." This sounds dismissive.
- "We pride ourselves on punctuality." This invites "well, not this time."
- Detailed tyre explanations. One sentence is plenty.
- "Please accept our sincere apologies for any inconvenience caused." This is generic, and "any" suggests you're not sure there was one.

You haven't done anything wrong here. A fair, warm reply like this is exactly the right response, and often wins back customers who will return.

# Monthly Budget (€1,454 income)

Running out around the 20th usually means the money isn't capped per week. Fixed costs are paid, then the rest gets spent freely until it's gone. This budget fixes that by giving you a **weekly allowance** instead of one big pot.

## 1. Income

| Source | Amount |
|---|---|
| BAföG | €934 |
| Minijob | €520 |
| **Total** | **€1,454** |

## 2. Fixed costs (pay these first)

| Item | Amount | Note |
|---|---|---|
| WG room (warm) | €480 | |
| Deutschlandticket | €58 | Check whether your Semesterticket already covers this |
| Health insurance | ~€140 | Only if you're not insured through your family. Your BAföG includes a surcharge for this. |
| Phone | ~€15 | |
| Semester fee reserve | ~€50 | ~€300 per semester, set aside monthly |
| Rundfunkbeitrag | €0 | BAföG recipients can apply for an exemption at rundfunkbeitrag.de |
| **Subtotal** | **~€743** | |

## 3. Savings (also pay first)

| Item | Amount |
|---|---|
| Emergency buffer | €100 |
| Irregular costs (clothes, gifts, repairs) | €40 |
| **Subtotal** | **€140** |

## 4. What's left for daily life

**€1,454 − €743 − €140 = €571 per month, which is about €130 per week**

This weekly €130 covers everything else:
- **Groceries:** ~€55
- **Drugstore and household:** ~€10
- **Eating out, going out, fun:** ~€50
- **Misc (coffee, small purchases):** ~€15

If you run out on Friday, you wait until Monday. That way a bad week only costs you a few days instead of the last 10 days of the month.

## How to make it work

2. **Know when your money arrives.** BAföG usually comes at the end of the month, and your minijob may pay on a different date. Make sure rent goes out right after the money comes in.
3. **Track every purchase for two weeks.** Even rough notes will do. Most people find one leak, often delivery food, small café or snack purchases, or subscriptions.
4. **Leave the buffer alone.** The €100 is only for real surprises, not for a short week.
