Q24-A.text:
# Garden Bed Plan: 3 m × 1.2 m

## How Many to Plant

| Plant | Number | Spacing | Space each |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Zucchini** | 1 | Needs about 1 m × 1 m | About 1 m² |
| **Tomatoes** | 3 | 60–65 cm apart, staked | About 0.5 m² |
| **Basil** | 6 | 25–30 cm apart | Small, fits in gaps |

**Zucchini** is the biggest space-taker. One healthy plant gives most households more than they can eat. Two would take about two-thirds of the bed and squeeze out the tomatoes.

**Tomatoes** fit at three if you grow them upright on stakes or in cages. If you let them sprawl, you'd only fit two.

**Basil** fits at six. Growing it under the tomatoes is a classic pairing, and the tomatoes give it a bit of afternoon shade in hot weather.

## Layout

```
|<--------------------------- 3.0 m --------------------------->|
+-----------------+---------------------------------------------+
|                 |                                             |
|                 |     T             T             T           |  ← back row (~40 cm in)
|        Z        |                                             |    tallest plants
|                 |                                             |
|                 |   B     B      B      B      B     B        |  ← front row (~30 cm in)
|                 |                                             |
+-----------------+---------------------------------------------+
      ~1.0 m                         ~2.0 m

Z = zucchini   T = tomato (staked)   B = basil
```

- **Put the tomatoes on the side away from the sun.** In the southern hemisphere, that's the south side, so they don't shade the basil. If the bed runs north–south, either side works.
- **Put the zucchini at the end with open space beside it**, such as a path or lawn. Its leaves can then spill over the edge instead of smothering the tomatoes.
- **Put stakes or cages in at planting time.** Doing it later can damage the roots.
- **Plant tomatoes deep**, burying about the bottom third of the stem. They grow roots along the buried stem, which helps them cope with less frequent watering.

## Watering Every Second Day

This works fine if you set the bed up to hold moisture.

1. **Mulch heavily.** Spread 5–7 cm of sugarcane mulch, straw or lucerne once the soil has warmed. This is the most important step.
2. **Water deeply, not lightly.** Soak the soil 20–30 cm down so roots grow deep. Once the plants are established in warm weather, that's roughly:
   - 10–15 L per tomato or zucchini
   - 2–3 L per basil plant
3. **Water in the early morning, at the base of the plants.** Wet leaves encourage powdery mildew on zucchini and blight on tomatoes. A drip line or soaker hose on a timer is ideal if your restrictions allow it.
4. **Add plenty of compost before planting.** Organic matter holds water much better than bare soil.
5. **Keep the moisture steady.** Tomatoes that swing between dry and wet get **blossom end rot**, which shows as black patches on the bottom of the fruit. Mulch plus deep watering prevents most of it.
6. **Check plants in the morning, not the afternoon.** Zucchini leaves often droop in the afternoon heat and recover overnight, which is normal. Basil is your early warning: if it's limp first thing in the morning, the bed needs more water.

## Quick Tips

- **Tomatoes:** Determinate or bush types are easier. If you grow indeterminate types, prune them to one or two main stems so they stay within their space.
- **Basil:** Pinch out the flower tips regularly to keep it bushy and productive.
- **Zucchini:** Pick fruit at about 15–20 cm. If you leave them, they turn into marrows almost overnight.

Q18-C.text:
# Saturday Tournament Rotation Plan

## The numbers

| | |
|---|---|
| Total match time | 4 matches × 30 min = **120 min** |
| Total player-minutes | 120 × 7 on the pitch = **840** |
| Goalkeeper minutes | 120 (only Tunde and Chidi can cover these) |
| Outfield player-minutes | 120 × 6 = **720**, shared by 16 outfield players |

**Result:**
- **Tunde and Chidi:** 60 minutes each, all in goal.
- **The other 16 players:** exactly 45 minutes each.

A perfect split would give everyone about 46.7 minutes. That isn't possible here. Only two players can keep goal, so they must cover 120 minutes between them, which means at least 60 each. This plan is the most even split available. The 15-minute gap is not favouritism, and it's worth saying so if a parent asks.

## How it works

1. **Split each half into two 7½-minute shifts.** That gives 16 shifts across the day.
2. **Put the 16 outfield players into 8 pairs (P1 to P8).**
3. **Three pairs (6 players) are on at a time.** At each change, all three pairs come off and the next three come on.
4. **Each pair plays 6 shifts of 7½ minutes, which is 45 minutes.** Every player gets 1 or 2 shifts in every match, so nobody sits out a whole game. Nobody plays two shifts in a row, so legs stay fresh. Every pair also starts at least one match.
5. **The keepers swap at half-time every match.** The one who starts alternates, so each keeper plays every match, starts two, and finishes two.

## The rotation

Changes happen at **7:30** and **half-time** in each half.

### Match 1 (GK: Tunde 1st half, Chidi 2nd half)
| Shift | On the pitch |
|---|---|
| 1st half, 0:00–7:30 | P1, P2, P3 |
| 1st half, 7:30–15:00 | P4, P5, P6 |
| 2nd half, 0:00–7:30 | P7, P8, P1 |
| 2nd half, 7:30–15:00 | P2, P3, P4 |

### Match 2 (GK: Chidi 1st half, Tunde 2nd half)
| Shift | On the pitch |
|---|---|
| 1st half, 0:00–7:30 | P5, P6, P7 |
| 1st half, 7:30–15:00 | P8, P1, P2 |
| 2nd half, 0:00–7:30 | P3, P4, P5 |
| 2nd half, 7:30–15:00 | P6, P7, P8 |

### Match 3 (GK: Tunde 1st half, Chidi 2nd half)
| Shift | On the pitch |
|---|---|
| 1st half, 0:00–7:30 | P7, P8, P1 |
| 1st half, 7:30–15:00 | P2, P3, P4 |
| 2nd half, 0:00–7:30 | P5, P6, P7 |
| 2nd half, 7:30–15:00 | P8, P1, P2 |

### Match 4 (GK: Chidi 1st half, Tunde 2nd half)
| Shift | On the pitch |
|---|---|
| 1st half, 0:00–7:30 | P3, P4, P5 |
| 1st half, 7:30–15:00 | P6, P7, P8 |
| 2nd half, 0:00–7:30 | P1, P2, P3 |
| 2nd half, 7:30–15:00 | P4, P5, P6 |

### Minutes check

| Pair | M1 | M2 | M3 | M4 | Total |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| P1 | 15 | 7½ | 15 | 7½ | **45** |
| P2 | 15 | 7½ | 15 | 7½ | **45** |
| P3 | 15 | 7½ | 7½ | 15 | **45** |
| P4 | 15 | 7½ | 7½ | 15 | **45** |
| P5 | 7½ | 15 | 7½ | 15 | **45** |
| P6 | 7½ | 15 | 7½ | 15 | **45** |
| P7 | 7½ | 15 | 15 | 7½ | **45** |
| P8 | 7½ | 15 | 15 | 7½ | **45** |
| Tunde (GK) | 15 | 15 | 15 | 15 | **60** |
| Chidi (GK) | 15 | 15 | 15 | 15 | **60** |

## Building the pairs

This is where you can make the plan work well on the pitch:

- **Pair one more defensive child with one more attacking child.** Any three pairs on together then give you three "back" players and three "front" players. That fits a **3-2-1** naturally: the three back players defend, and the three front players form two midfielders and a striker.
- **Spread your strongest players across different pairs.** Don't put two of them together. Because the pairs mix in different combinations all day, every line-up stays reasonably balanced.
- **Consider friendships.** Kids who get on well often play better together, but avoid pairing two who distract each other.
- **Optional, for development:** have partners swap roles in Matches 3 and 4, so the defender gets a go up front and vice versa.

## Matchday logistics

- **Check the tournament rules before Saturday.** You need rolling substitutions and re-entry to be allowed, which is standard in most youth tournaments. If subs only happen at stoppages, make the change at the first stoppage after about 7:00. The odd 30 seconds either way won't matter.
- **Get a helper parent with a stopwatch** to call the 7:30 change. It's very easy to lose track while coaching.
- **Have the next three pairs ready on the touchline before 7:30,** with bibs on and shin pads in, so the change is quick.
- **Print the four tables and give a copy to your helper,** or write them on a whiteboard. Tell the kids their pair number in advance, so you only need to call "P4, P5, P6 on!"
- **Use the keeper who isn't in goal as your emergency outfield sub** for injuries or a child who's unwell, and have them warm up before their half in goal. Otherwise, keep them out of the outfield rotation, because using them there takes minutes from the 16.

## If things go wrong

- **An outfield player is absent or injured:** their partner still plays the pair's shifts. Cover the missing player's slots with players from pairs that are resting. Use a different child each time, ideally ones in a match where they only had one shift. Those children each gain 7½ minutes, so the spread stays tight.
- **A keeper is absent or injured:** the other keeper would have to play all 120 minutes, which is a lot to ask. **Pick an emergency third keeper now,** even someone who's just willing, and give them a few minutes in goal at training this week.
- **Two players can't make it:** the gaps are 12 shifts. Spread them across the resting pairs in the same way, so each covering child gains no more than one extra shift.
- **You reach a knockout match:** carry on the cycle from wherever you finished.
- **Subs are only allowed at half-time:** use the same pair order, but each "shift" becomes a full half. Each pair plays 3 halves, which is still 45 minutes. The downside is that two pairs will sit out one entire match, so it's worth arguing for rolling subs.

## Wellbeing on a four-match day

- Make sure every child has a full water bottle, and bring snacks for between matches, such as fruit or cereal bars.
- Keep resting players warm, especially if it's cold. A coat on the bench is fine.
- Run a short warm-up before each match, not just the first one.
- Tell the kids, and the parents, that **everyone plays the same amount whatever the score.** It takes pressure off and avoids awkward conversations later.

Q15-C.text:
# Berlin → Lisbon Moving Checklist: 17 Nov 2026 to Movers on Sat 9 Jan 2027

You have about 7½ weeks, and the Christmas and New Year period sits right in the middle. German offices, vets and many businesses slow down or close from about 23 Dec to 4 Jan. So the plan front-loads anything official or time-sensitive into November and early December.

**Assumptions:**
- You fly within a day or two of 9 Jan.
- Your Berlin lease ends on or after move day.
- You're both EU citizens.

If either of you isn't an EU citizen, the Portuguese residence steps are different and need their own plan.

---

## ⚠️ The critical path: Mochi's paperwork (do this week)

For travel within the EU, a cat needs three things:
1. **An ISO microchip**, implanted before or at the same time as the rabies vaccination.
2. **A valid rabies vaccination** recorded in the passport.
3. **An EU pet passport** filled in by an authorised vet.

No titre test or tapeworm treatment is needed for cats moving Germany → Portugal.

The trap is the rabies date:
- **If the vaccination is still valid** (check the "valid until" date in the passport), a booster given before it expires keeps cover continuous. You can travel immediately.
- **If it has lapsed**, the new shot counts as a primary vaccination. Mochi can't travel until **21 days after it**. To fly about 9–10 Jan, that shot must happen by about **18 Dec** at the absolute latest. Realistically, aim for November, because vets get booked up before the holidays.

Also have the vet **scan the chip** and confirm it matches the number in the passport. A mismatch or unreadable chip is the most common way pets get stopped.

---

## Week 1: Tue 17 – Sun 22 Nov · Bookings and the things that can't slip

**Mochi**
- [ ] Open the pet passport and note the chip number, rabies vaccination date and "valid until" date.
- [ ] Book a vet appointment for this week or next. Purposes: chip scan, passport check, booster if due, general health check, and advice on travel stress.

**Flights**
- [ ] Book flights that allow a **cat in the cabin**.
  - Ryanair and easyJet don't take pets.
  - TAP and Lufthansa Group airlines generally do, usually up to about 8 kg including the carrier, with a limited number of pet spots per flight.
  - **Confirm the pet booking before or as you pay.** Spots fill up.
- [ ] Weigh Mochi plus a typical carrier to make sure you're under the limit.

**Movers**
- [ ] Confirm the date, arrival time and estimated volume.
- [ ] Confirm whether they pack for you or you self-pack, and whether they supply boxes.
- [ ] Confirm transit insurance and the delivery window in Lisbon. It's often several days later, and you'll be living out of suitcases until then.
- [ ] Ask whether they arrange the **Halteverbotszone** (temporary no-parking zone) in Berlin. If not, you'll apply in Week 3–4.
- [ ] Ask about access at the Lisbon end: narrow streets, stairs, lift size. Some Lisbon addresses need a smaller shuttle van, which costs extra.

**Housing**
- [ ] Berlin: confirm the lease end date, notice status and a **handover appointment** (Wohnungsübergabe) with the landlord.
- [ ] Check your lease for end-of-tenancy duties such as painting, removing fixtures or restoring the kitchen.
- [ ] Lisbon: ask the landlord for a **full inventory with photos**: kitchenware, bedding, towels, washing machine, iron, hoover, etc. This decides what you ship.

**Selling furniture**
- [ ] List the **sofa** now on Kleinanzeigen and Facebook Marketplace. December demand is softer, so give yourselves time.
- [ ] List the **bed** for collection on about 8–9 Jan, or decide to sell it earlier and sleep on an air mattress.

**General**
- [ ] Start a shared master list or spreadsheet covering tasks, contracts to cancel, and notice periods.
- [ ] Check both passports and IDs are valid well beyond the move.

---

## Week 2: Mon 23 – Sun 29 Nov · Vet visit, give notice, start decluttering

**Mochi**
- [ ] Vet visit happens: chip scanned, passport checked, booster done if needed. Keep the passport with your travel documents from now on.
- [ ] Ask the vet about travel stress. Some vets prescribe gabapentin for cats. Airlines generally don't accept sedated pets, so follow vet advice rather than improvising.
- [ ] Buy an **airline-compliant soft carrier** if you don't have one. Leave it open in the living room with a blanket and treats so it becomes familiar.
- [ ] Buy a **harness and lead**. At airport security you have to take the cat out of the carrier.

**Cancellations** (give notice now so end dates line up with mid-January)
- [ ] **Internet**: moving abroad lets you end the contract early, generally with one month's notice. Ask how to return the router; many providers charge if you don't.
- [ ] **Electricity / gas**: give your move-out date. You'll submit final meter readings on handover day.
- [ ] **Hausrat (contents) insurance**: ask whether it ends with the move abroad or covers the move itself.
- [ ] **Haftpflicht (liability insurance)**: check whether it still covers you living in Portugal. Many German policies don't.
- [ ] Gym, streaming and other subscriptions, mobile contracts (or keep a German number if useful for banking 2FA), magazines, Amazon address.

**Admin**
- [ ] Plan your **Abmeldung** (deregistration). In Berlin you can do it online with eID, or by post or in person. It's allowed from **one week before** you move out, so from 2 Jan. Put it in the calendar now.
- [ ] Set up **Deutsche Post forwarding** (Nachsendeauftrag) to your Lisbon address. International forwarding is available. Start it from about 9 Jan.

**Decluttering**
- [ ] Start with storage: Keller, cupboards, under the bed, the back of wardrobes.
- [ ] Sort everything into **Move / Suitcase / Sell / Donate / Bin**. Since the Lisbon flat is furnished, be ruthless with bulky items it already has.

---

## Week 3: Mon 30 Nov – Sun 6 Dec · Sell, sort, set up Lisbon

**Selling and disposal**
- [ ] Push the sofa sale: lower the price, repost, offer weekend collection.
- [ ] Sell or donate other items (books, kitchen duplicates, lamps) via Kleinanzeigen, neighbourhood groups or charity shops.
- [ ] **Book a BSR Sperrmüll collection as a backup** for the sofa or bed in case sales fall through. Book now, because December slots and holiday closures make it hard later. The BSR recycling centres are another option.

**Packing**
- [ ] If self-packing, get boxes, tape, markers and bubble wrap.
- [ ] Pack the things you won't need for 5 weeks: books, decor, out-of-season clothes, keepsakes.
- [ ] Number every box and label it with the **destination room in Lisbon** and a short contents list. Keep an inventory with photos.

**Lisbon set-up**
- [ ] Confirm what's included in the rent: electricity, water, gas, internet. If you set them up yourself, start now. Portuguese installs can take a while, especially over the holidays.
- [ ] Make sure you both have a **NIF** (Portuguese tax number). You likely needed it for the lease.
- [ ] Find a vet near the new flat.

**Documents**
- [ ] Make one physical folder plus digital scans of: passports, lease contracts (old and new), pet passport, work contracts, payslips, tax documents, insurance policies, birth or marriage certificates, and medical and prescription records.

---

## Week 4: Mon 7 – Sun 13 Dec · Parking permit, deeper packing

- [ ] **Halteverbotszone**: if the movers aren't arranging it, apply to your Bezirk's road traffic authority now. Allow at least 2–3 weeks, and longer with holidays. Signs usually have to go up a few days beforehand.
- [ ] **Deutschlandticket**: you must cancel by the 10th to end the subscription at the end of that month. Cancel by 10 Dec for it to end 31 Dec, or by 10 Jan for it to end 31 Jan.
- [ ] The sofa should be sold or booked for collection by now.
- [ ] Pack the spare room, hallway, decor and anything non-daily.
- [ ] Start **eating down the freezer and pantry**. Movers won't take perishables, and usually won't take liquids, aerosols, paint, gas canisters or plants.
- [ ] Start updating your address with your bank, employer, Krankenkasse, Rentenversicherung (keep your number) and Finanzamt. Set the Lisbon address effective from your move date.
- [ ] Find out whether you need a final German tax return for the partial year.

---

## Week 5: Mon 14 – Sun 20 Dec · Last "offices are open" week

Treat this as your hard deadline for anything that needs a German office, vet, landlord or company to respond.

- [ ] **Mochi**: if a new primary rabies shot was needed and somehow hasn't happened, this is the absolute last moment. Otherwise just confirm the passport is complete and stamped.
- [ ] Reconfirm the movers in writing: date, time, address, phone numbers, parking, Lisbon delivery window and any items they won't carry.
- [ ] Confirm the Berlin handover appointment and the Lisbon key handover.
- [ ] Decide **where Mochi will be on move day**: a friend's flat, a cattery, or a closed bathroom with a "DO NOT OPEN — CAT" sign. Book it if it's a cattery or sitter.
- [ ] Decide where **you sleep on 9 Jan** if the bed is gone and you fly the next day: a friend's place or a hotel near BER.
- [ ] Chase any cancellation confirmations you haven't received.

---

## Week 6: Mon 21 – Sun 27 Dec · Christmas (light week)

- [ ] Pack as you go between celebrations: decorations go straight into boxes after use.
- [ ] Keep eating down the food.
- [ ] Pack the kitchen except a minimal set: 2 plates, cutlery, a pan, mugs.
- [ ] Keep Mochi's routine stable. A flat full of boxes is already stressful for a cat.

---

## Week 7: Mon 28 Dec – Sun 3 Jan · Final packing push and Silvester

- [ ] **31 Dec**: Berlin fireworks are extreme. Keep Mochi indoors in a quiet room with windows closed and curtains drawn. Treat this as a dry run for move-day stress.
- [ ] From **2 Jan**: do the **Abmeldung**, online or with an appointment, and get the **Abmeldebestätigung**. You'll need it to cancel the Rundfunkbeitrag and some contracts.
- [ ] Pack every room except the essentials (see the "Open first" list below).
- [ ] Pack your **suitcases** for the gap before your shipment arrives in Lisbon. Lisbon flats are often cold and damp in January with little central heating, so bring warm layers, slippers and maybe a hot-water bottle.
- [ ] Confirm the bed buyer's collection time and take a deposit if you can.

---

## Week 8: Mon 4 – Fri 8 Jan · Final week

- [ ] Clean the flat: fill holes, remove anything not in the lease, and do any painting the lease requires.
- [ ] Defrost and clean the fridge or freezer if you own one and it's being moved or sold.
- [ ] Take apart anything the movers won't, and keep screws in labelled bags taped to the item.
- [ ] Return or arrange return of the router and other rental devices once internet ends.
- [ ] Take cash, keys, chargers, documents and valuables out of the "movers" zone.
- [ ] Prepare **Mochi's travel kit**:
  - pet passport
  - carrier with an absorbent pad and a familiar blanket
  - harness and lead
  - a few days of food
  - travel litter tray with a small bag of litter
  - collapsible bowl
  - Feliway spray
  - any vet-prescribed medication
- [ ] **Bed**: collection on 8 Jan evening, or after the movers on 9 Jan.

---

## 🚚 Move Day: Saturday 9 Jan

- [ ] **Secure Mochi first**, before the door is opened for the movers: at the sitter's, or shut in with food, water, litter and a sign.
- [ ] Walk the movers through: what goes, what stays, and what's fragile.
- [ ] Check their inventory list against your box numbers, sign it, and keep a copy.
- [ ] After loading, check every cupboard, drawer, the balcony and the Keller.
- [ ] **Photograph the meter readings** (electricity, gas, water) and the flat's condition.
- [ ] Handover with the landlord, if today: sign the protocol, return all keys, give your IBAN for the deposit (Kaution) refund. Landlords can keep part of it until the next utility cost statement.

---

## ✈️ Flight Day with Mochi

- [ ] Small meal several hours before the flight, not right before. Offer water.
- [ ] Have the passport ready at check-in. The airline may ask for it.
- [ ] At security, take Mochi out (harness on) and put the carrier through the scanner.
- [ ] Keep the carrier under the seat in front of you, closed for the whole flight.

---

## 🧳 Carry Yourselves (never with the movers)

- Passports, IDs, pet passport, both leases, keys to the new flat
- Laptops, phones, chargers, hard drives
- Jewellery, cash, cards
- Medication and prescriptions
- An **"Open first" bag** for the days before the shipment arrives:
  - bedding and towels if the flat doesn't have them
  - a basic toolkit
  - toiletries
  - a few changes of clothes
  - kettle or coffee gear

Portugal uses the same Type F plugs as Germany, so no adapters are needed.

---

## 🇵🇹 After Arrival (first 2–6 weeks)

**Mochi**
- [ ] Set up one quiet "base room" first with litter, food, water and hiding spots, then let Mochi explore gradually.
- [ ] **Register Mochi in SIAC**, Portugal's pet database, through a local vet. Registration is mandatory for cats, so do it in the first few weeks.
- [ ] Update the chip registration (TASSO, Findefix, etc.) with your Lisbon address.

**Germany**
- [ ] Deregister from the **Rundfunkbeitrag** online using the Abmeldebestätigung.
- [ ] Pay the final utility bills and confirm the deposit refund.
- [ ] Check that forwarded post is arriving.

**Portugal**
- [ ] **EU citizen registration (CRUE)** at the Câmara Municipal: required if you stay longer than 3 months.
- [ ] Register with Social Security (**NISS**) if you'll work there.
- [ ] Register at your local health centre for a **número de utente** (SNS).
- [ ] Open a Portuguese bank account and get a local SIM.
- [ ] Check the flat against the landlord's inventory and report any damage within the agreed period.
- [ ] Unpack the shipment and check it against the movers' inventory. Report damage quickly, as the insurance deadlines are short.

---

### Things to tell me so I can tighten this up
1. **Your flight date.** It changes the Mochi deadlines and where you sleep on 9 Jan.
2. **Your Berlin lease end date and handover date.**
3. **Whether the movers pack for you.** If so, Weeks 3–7 get much lighter.
4. **Mochi's rabies "valid until" date.** This tells us whether the 21-day wait applies.

Q24-B.text:
# Planting Plan for Your 3 m × 1.2 m Bed

Since it's spring in November, I've assumed you're in the Southern Hemisphere, where the sun sits to the north. Tall plants go on the **south** side so they don't shade shorter ones.

## How Many of Each

| Plant | Number | Spacing | Area used |
|---|---|---|---|
| Zucchini (bush type) | **1** | Needs about 1 m × 1 m | 1.0 m of bed length |
| Tomatoes (staked) | **3** | 60 cm apart | Back row of the remaining 2.0 m |
| Basil | **6** | 30 cm apart | Front row of the remaining 2.0 m |

**Why only one zucchini?** One bush zucchini fills a full 1 m × 1 m. A second would cut you to 1 tomato. One plant at peak still gives several fruit a week.

**Why 3 tomatoes, not 4?** Four would fit at 50 cm spacing. But with watering only every second day, the wider 60 cm spacing means less competition for water and better airflow against disease.

## Layout

Measurements run along the 3 m length from the left end. The front edge faces north.

```
SOUTH (back)
 0 m        1.0 m                                    3.0 m
 +----------+----------------------------------------+
 |          |    T          T          T             |  ← tomatoes 0.9 m from front edge
 |    Z     |   (1.4)     (2.0)      (2.6)           |     (0.3 m from back edge)
 |  (0.5)   |                                        |
 |          |                                        |
 |          |  B    B    B    B    B    B            |  ← basil 0.25 m from front edge
 |          |(1.25)(1.55)(1.85)(2.15)(2.45)(2.75)    |
 +----------+----------------------------------------+
NORTH (front, sunny side)                        1.2 m deep
```

- **Zucchini:** 1 plant, centred 0.5 m from the left end and 0.6 m from the front. It sprawls to fill the whole left metre.
- **Tomatoes:** at 1.4 m, 2.0 m and 2.6 m along, 0.9 m from the front edge. Put a 1.8 m stake or cage in at planting. Prune each plant to 1 or 2 main stems so they stay within their 60 cm.
- **Basil:** at 1.25, 1.55, 1.85, 2.15, 2.45 and 2.75 m along, 0.25 m from the front edge. This keeps the basil in full sun, 65 cm clear of the tomato stems, and outside the zucchini's spread.

## Watering Every Second Day

1. **Mulch 5–7 cm deep** straight after planting, using sugar cane, pea straw or similar. Keep it 5 cm back from the stems. This is the biggest single help with your restriction.
2. **Water deeply in the early morning** on your watering days, at the base of each plant rather than over the leaves. Once the plants are established, roughly:
   - Zucchini: 8–10 L
   - Each tomato: 4–5 L (12–15 L total)
   - Each basil: about 1 L (6 L total)
   - **Total: about 30 L per watering.** For the first two weeks, use about half that, since the seedlings' roots are small.
3. **Water evenly.** Tomatoes and zucchini get blossom end rot when soil swings between wet and dry. A deep soak plus mulch keeps moisture steady between your watering days.
4. **Before planting**, dig 2–3 buckets of compost through the whole bed. It helps the soil hold water much longer.
5. **During heatwaves above about 35 °C**, a piece of 30–50% shade cloth over the basil and tomatoes on hot afternoons cuts water loss a lot.

## Planting Notes for This Month

- Plant **tomatoes and zucchini as seedlings**, not seed, to get the most from the season.
- Plant tomatoes deep, burying the stem up to the first set of leaves. They grow extra roots along the buried stem, which helps them handle drier days.
- Basil sulks if nights drop below about 10 °C. If your nights are still cool, plant the tomatoes and zucchini now and add the basil 1–2 weeks later.
- 6 hours of full sun is enough for all three. Tomatoes and zucchini will fruit well, and basil will thrive.

Q23-C.text:
# Data Science vs. Biotechnology: A Decision Framework for You

You have about 18 days until 5 December. That's enough time to decide well if you use it deliberately.

## The short answer

**On the facts you've given, the BSc in Data Science looks like the stronger choice.** There is one big condition: you need at least a neutral-to-positive interest in working with data, code and logic. If you love biology and would be miserable doing programming, the answer changes. Here's why I lean this way, and what could flip it.

---

## 1. What your marks tell you

| Subject | Score | What it suggests |
|---|---|---|
| Maths | 92% | A real strength. Data science uses statistics, linear algebra and probability heavily, so this is a direct advantage. |
| Biology | 78% | Solid, but clearly not your strongest area. |

**Caveat:** marks measure aptitude and exam performance, not passion. Plenty of people score 78% in a subject they love because of one bad paper or a weak teacher. Ask yourself honestly which subject you'd study if there were no exam at all.

Also worth knowing: biotech is not maths-free (biostatistics, bioprocess calculations), and data science is not biology-free if you later go into health or bio data. So the skills overlap more than the course names suggest.

---

## 2. Cost and time

Assuming fees are near your ₹2.5 lakh/year ceiling (please check the actual figures):

| | Data Science (3 yrs) | Biotechnology (4 yrs) |
|---|---|---|
| Tuition (at ₹2.5L/yr) | ~₹7.5 lakh | ~₹10 lakh |
| Living/hostel costs | 3 years | 4 years |
| Start earning | ~1 year earlier | 1 year later |
| **Effective difference** | — | ~₹2.5L extra fees + extra living costs + ~1 year of lost salary |

The real gap is likely **₹5–8 lakh or more** once you count the lost year of income. But the 4th year isn't necessarily wasted. Under the NEP framework, a 4-year honours or research degree can let you go straight into a PhD or a 1-year master's at some institutions. Ask the college exactly what the 4th year gives you.

Also check:
- Does the ₹2.5L ceiling include hostel, mess, exam fees, lab fees and books? Biotech often has higher lab and consumable fees.
- Are fee hikes likely over 3–4 years?
- Can you get a scholarship? Your 92% in maths may qualify you for merit fee waivers. Ask directly.

---

## 3. Career prospects

### Data Science
**Strengths**
- Demand exists across many sectors: tech, finance, e-commerce, healthcare, consulting, government.
- You can get entry-level analyst roles straight after a BSc (data analyst, business analyst, junior data scientist).
- Skills are portable. If you change your mind later, Python, SQL and statistics transfer to many fields.
- Your maths strength gives you an edge.

**Risks, honestly stated**
- **Competition is intense.** You'll compete with BTech CSE graduates, engineers from every branch, and people who did online certifications.
- **The college brand and your portfolio matter a lot.** A BSc from a lesser-known college with no projects or internships struggles. The degree alone isn't enough.
- **AI is changing entry-level work.** Routine reporting and basic analysis are being automated. People who combine statistics, domain knowledge and communication will do better than those who only know tools.
- Many "data science" BSc programs are newly launched and of uneven quality. Check the curriculum carefully.

### Biotechnology
**Strengths**
- Meaningful work in pharma, vaccines, diagnostics, agriculture, food and research.
- India has a large and growing biopharma and biosimilars sector.
- It's a good foundation if you're aiming for research or a PhD, including abroad.

**Risks, honestly stated**
- **A biotech bachelor's alone usually leads to modest outcomes in India.** Typical roles are lab technician, QC/QA, or clinical research associate, often at modest starting salaries.
- **Most good biotech careers need an MSc and often a PhD.** That means 4 years plus 2 years plus possibly 5 more, so you should budget for further study.
- Industry placements at the bachelor's level are often weak outside top institutions.

### Rough comparison (varies a lot by college and city)
| | Data Science | Biotechnology |
|---|---|---|
| Employable straight after bachelor's | Moderately yes | Limited |
| Typical path to a good job | BSc + strong projects/internships (MSc optional) | BSc + MSc (+ PhD for research roles) |
| Total years to a solid career | ~3–5 | ~6–10 |
| Fit with your strongest subject | High | Moderate |

*Treat any salary figures you hear, including from colleges, with caution. Ask for median placement figures, not the highest package.*

---

## 4. Ways to combine both

You don't have to give up one field entirely.

- **Data Science → Bioinformatics / Computational Biology / Health Data.** You can do an MSc in bioinformatics or work in health-tech, genomics or pharma analytics. Biology knowledge plus data skills is a valuable mix, and your 78% biology is perfectly adequate for this.
- **Biotech + coding.** If you choose biotech, learning Python and statistics alongside it makes you far more employable. Bioinformatics roles favour biotech graduates who can code.

Path 1 is generally easier, because learning applied biology later is easier than learning serious maths and programming later.

---

## 5. What would change my recommendation

**Choose Biotechnology if:**
- You're genuinely fascinated by biology (genetics, diseases, lab work) and find coding dull or stressful.
- You're aiming for research, a PhD, or science abroad, and your family is comfortable with a longer path to earning.
- The biotech program at this college is clearly stronger (faculty, labs, placements, research links) than its data science program.
- The 4th year gives you a real advantage, such as direct PhD eligibility or a strong research thesis.

**Choose Data Science if:**
- You enjoy problem-solving, logic and maths, and are open to coding.
- You want to become financially independent sooner.
- You want flexibility to move across industries later.
- The program has a solid curriculum and real placement results.

---

## 6. What to check about this college before 5 December

These questions matter as much as the choice of subject. A good biotech program can beat a weak data science program.

**For both programs**
1. **Placement data:** what share of the last batch was placed, the *median* package, and which companies hired. If the data science program is new and has no graduated batch, that's a risk to note.
2. **Accreditation:** NAAC grade, UGC recognition, university affiliation.
3. **Full fee breakdown** for every year, including hostel and other charges.
4. **Refund policy** if you withdraw early or switch.
5. **Whether you can switch programs** after the first semester or year.

**For Data Science specifically**
- Does the syllabus include statistics, probability, linear algebra, Python, SQL, machine learning, and real projects?
- Is there a compulsory internship?
- Are the faculty qualified in statistics or computer science, or reassigned from unrelated departments?

**For Biotechnology specifically**
- Are the labs well equipped, and how much hands-on lab time do you get?
- Are there industry tie-ups or research internships?
- What does the 4th year include (research project, honours, PhD eligibility)?
- Where did past graduates go (jobs, MSc programs, PhDs)?

**Best source:** talk to 2–3 current students or recent graduates of each program. LinkedIn is a good way to find them. They'll tell you what the brochure won't.

---

## 7. A plan for the next 18 days

| Dates | Task |
|---|---|
| **17–21 Nov** | Self-check: try a free beginner Python or statistics lesson for a few hours, and read about one biotech topic you like. Notice which one you *want* to keep going with. |
| **19–25 Nov** | Get the answers to the college questions above. Visit or call the department, and contact alumni. |
| **25–28 Nov** | Sit down with your parents and go through cost, timelines and outcomes together. |
| **By 1 Dec** | Decide, leaving a buffer before the deadline for documents, fee payment and any portal problems. |

---

## Bottom line

- **Your profile (strong maths, 3-year duration, lower total cost, earlier earning, broader job options) favours Data Science.**
- **Biotech makes sense mainly if biology is your real passion and you're willing to commit to a longer path through an MSc or PhD.**
- **If you're unsure, Data Science keeps more doors open**, including a later move into bioinformatics or health data, where your biology background still counts.
- Whichever you choose, **the quality of the program and what you do during it (projects, internships, skills) will matter more than the degree title.**

If you tell me the college name, the exact fees, and what you enjoy (or dread) about each subject, I can give you a sharper recommendation.

Q26-B.text:
# Daily Baking Plan

## Weekdays: bake 65, down from 80

You sell about 65 (80 baked − 15 left). Plan for that, with one flexible batch so you can respond to busy days.

| Batch | Loaves | When |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 20 | Before opening |
| 2 | 20 | Before opening |
| 3 | 20 | Out of the oven by mid-morning |
| 4 (top-up) | 5 (up to 10 on a busy day) | Late morning, decided by a stock check |

**The late-morning check:** Count what's on the shelf. If roughly half of the first 60 are gone, bake 5 more. If sales are clearly running ahead, bake 10. If it's slow, skip it.

**Result:** You cut about 15 wasted loaves a day down to 0–5. That's roughly 50–75 fewer loaves thrown out per week.

## Saturdays: bake 140, up from 120

Selling out by 1pm means you're losing afternoon customers, so you don't yet know your real Saturday demand. Add one batch and use it to find out.

| Batch | Loaves | When |
|---|---|---|
| 1–4 | 80 | Before opening and early morning |
| 5 | 20 | Mid-morning |
| 6 | 20 | Out of the oven by about 11:30am |
| 7 (new) | 20 | Out of the oven by about 12:45pm, before you'd normally sell out |

Spacing the later batches keeps fresh bread coming through the rush instead of front-loading it.

## Adjust after 3–4 Saturdays

- **Still sold out before closing:** go to 160 (8 batches) and put the extra batch in early afternoon.
- **Sold out near closing:** 140 is right.
- **More than about 10 left:** cut the 7th batch to 10 loaves, for 130 total.

## Weekly totals

| | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| Weekdays (5 days) | 400 baked, ~75 wasted | 325–350 baked, ~0–25 wasted |
| Saturday | 120, sold out at 1pm | 140, open later into the afternoon |

For the next two weeks, jot down each day's leftovers and the time you sell out. That will show you whether 65 is right or whether some weekdays, like Fridays, need their own number.

| **Savings** | | |
| Emergency fund | 219 | Build to €1,000–1,500, then use part of it for goals (travel, laptop). |
| **Total** | **1,454** ✅ | |

### Check these possible costs

- **Health insurance:** If you're 25 or older, or not family-insured through your parents, you pay the student rate of roughly **€140/month** for health and long-term care insurance. BAföG includes a supplement for this, so if your €934 includes that supplement, you are probably paying insurance. In that case, **take it out of the savings line** (€219 becomes about €79).
- **Rundfunkbeitrag (€18.36):** In a WG, only one person pays and it's usually split among flatmates. If you pay it yourself, BAföG recipients can apply for an exemption at rundfunkbeitrag.de. Take any share you do pay out of savings.
- **Internet:** If it's not included in your warm rent, add your WG share.

---

## 3. The Weekly System

Most people run out of money mid-month because they see one big balance and spend from it freely. The fix is to **never let yourself see the whole month's money at once.**

### Setup (one evening)
1. **Use two accounts:**
   - **Main account:** income arrives here and fixed costs leave from here.
   - **Spending account:** a free second account or sub-account (many banks offer "Spaces" or "Unterkonten"). Only your weekly money goes here.
2. **Pay your savings first:** On payday, set up a standing order that moves the savings and irregular-cost money (€294) into a separate savings account. Don't wait to save "what's left," because nothing will be left.
3. **Pay yourself weekly:** Set a standing order of **€125 every Monday** from your main account to your spending account.
4. **Pay for daily life only with the spending account's card.**

### Rules
- When the €125 is gone, that week's spending is over. You wait until Monday.
- Money left on Sunday rolls over into next week or goes to savings.
- Never top up the spending account from savings during the week. That one rule makes the system work.

### A typical €125 week

| | € |
|---|---|
| Groceries (Aldi/Lidl/Netto, share basics with the WG) | 55 |
| Mensa / coffee / snacks | 25 |
| Going out, hobbies, fun | 35 |
| Drugstore & household | 10 |

---

## 4. Payday Timing

Your two incomes probably arrive at different times:

- **BAföG** is usually paid at the **end of the month for the next month**, which is when spending often goes wrong.
- **Minijob pay** often arrives at the start or middle of the month.

Because your fixed costs come out early and your spending comes out evenly week by week, the timing no longer matters. You just need **one month's buffer** in the main account so the standing orders never fail. Use your first month or two of savings to build that cushion.

---

## 5. Find Your Leak (first 2 weeks)

Before or while starting, look at your **last two bank statements** and highlight anything that isn't rent or your ticket. The usual student leaks:

| Leak | Typical monthly cost |
|---|---|
| Lieferando / Wolt / Uber Eats | €80–200 |
| Daily café coffee + snacks | €60–120 |
| Späti / kiosk / late-night food | €40–100 |
| Online shopping, small Amazon orders | €50–150 |
| **Klarna / PayPal "pay later"** | Hidden, and it eats next month's money |
| Forgotten subscriptions | €10–40 |

If you use buy-now-pay-later, **stop using it and pay off what's open first**. It's one of the most common reasons money disappears before the month ends.

---

## 6. Ways to Spend Less

**Food (your biggest flexible cost):**
- Eat at the Mensa: a full meal for about €3–5 is hard to beat.
- Plan 3–4 meals per week and shop once with a list.
- Cook big batches (pasta, curry, chili) and freeze portions.
- Use **Too Good To Go** and look for reduced-price stickers in the evening.
- Split basics (oil, spices, rice, toilet paper) with your WG.
- You work at a café, so ask whether staff get free drinks or leftovers.

**Other:**
- Look for student discounts (ISIC, UNiDAYS, cinema student days, free museum days).
- Cancel subscriptions you didn't use in the last month.
- Use the 24-hour rule: wait a day before any non-essential purchase over €30.

---

## 7. BAföG and Minijob

- Your €520 minijob should be within the earnings allowance for BAföG, which is currently tied to the minijob limit. Still, **always report your job to your BAföG office**, and check the current limit before working extra shifts (for example, over Christmas). Going over it can lead to repayment demands.
- If your situation changes (rent, insurance, parents' income), you can **apply for a recalculation**. You may be entitled to more.

---

## 8. Your First Month

| When | What |
|---|---|
| **This week** | Go through your last 2 statements, find your leaks, cancel what you don't need. |
| **This week** | Open a free second account or sub-account. |
| **Next payday** | Set up standing orders: savings (€294) and weekly money (€125 every Monday). |
| **Every Sunday (5 min)** | Check what's left in the spending account and what's coming up next week. |
| **End of month** | Review: did anything break the budget? Adjust categories, but keep the total the same. |

### If you run short this month
Since you're already short before your new system starts: buy groceries for the remaining days first, cook from what's in your cupboard, and skip anything optional until your next payday. Then start the system cleanly.

---

## Summary

- You have **€916 after fixed costs**, which is enough for a comfortable student month.
- **Move savings out on payday** and **give yourself €125 every Monday**.
- When the weekly money is gone, you wait until Monday.
- Check whether you pay **health insurance** and adjust savings if so.
- Within 2–3 months you should have money left at the end of the month and a growing emergency fund.

If you share your actual spending from last month, even roughly, I can adjust the categories to fit how you really live.

Q27-A.text:
# Can You Afford Heated Floors?

**Short answer: Not comfortably as things stand.**

| Item | Cost (CAD) |
|---|---|
| Base quote (labour + basic materials) | 11,200 |
| Heated floors | 2,400 |
| **Subtotal** | **13,600** |
| **Remaining from 14,000** | **400 (about 3%)** |

For bathroom renovations, a contingency of **10–20%** is standard. On a 13,600 job that's roughly **1,400–2,700**. Bathrooms are especially prone to surprises because opening walls and floors often reveals water damage, rot, mould, old plumbing, or wiring that isn't up to code. With only 400 left, one surprise could push you over budget mid-project.

## Check the Quote First

Ask your contractor these questions. The answers could change everything:

1. **Does 11,200 include tax?** GST/HST adds 5–15% depending on your province. If tax isn't included, you're already at roughly 12,500–13,000 before heated floors.
2. **What do "basic materials" cover?** Often they don't include the vanity, toilet, faucets, showerhead, tub or shower glass, mirror, lighting, exhaust fan, or accessories. These can easily total 1,500–4,000+.
3. **What does the 2,400 for heated floors include?** Check whether it covers the electrician, a dedicated circuit, and the thermostat (a programmable or smart one adds 150–400). Also ask whether your electrical panel has capacity, since a panel upgrade would be a big extra.
4. **Is a permit needed, and who pays for it?** Plumbing and electrical work often require one.
5. **What's the payment schedule, and how are change orders priced?**

## Other Costs to Budget For

- **Living without your only bathroom for 3+ weeks.** This is a real cost. Options include a gym membership for showers, a portable toilet rental, staying with family, or a short-term rental for part of the time. Ask whether the contractor can keep the toilet working for as long as possible, or reinstall it temporarily at the end of each day. Also plan for **delays**, since 3 weeks can easily become 4–5, especially in January.
- **Winter timing.** Cold weather can slow material deliveries and drying or curing times for mortar and grout.
- **Small extras:** paint, trim, outlets/GFCI, caulking, disposal fees, and possibly drywall repair in adjoining rooms.

## Ways to Make Heated Floors Work

- **Heat only part of the floor.** Covering just the area in front of the vanity and shower/tub, where you actually stand, can significantly reduce the cost.
- **Save between now and January 5.** You have about 7 weeks. Even an extra 1,000–1,500 would give you a reasonable buffer.
- **Choose cheaper finishes.** Mid-range tile and a stock vanity instead of custom can free up 1,000+.
- **Supply fixtures yourself** if the contractor allows it. Boxing Day sales fall just before your start date.
- **Rough in now, install later.** This is less useful for heated floors, since the mat goes under the tile. But you could at least have the electrician run the dedicated circuit now so a future retrofit is easier.

## Suggested Rule

Go ahead with heated floors **only if** you confirm the 11,200 includes tax and fixtures, **and** you can keep at least **1,400** set aside as contingency. If not, consider partial-coverage heating or trimming elsewhere. Heated floors are wonderful, but running out of money with an open wall in your only bathroom is much worse.

If you share what the contractor says about tax and what's included, I can put together a full line-by-line budget for you.

**I'd keep the $5,000 as a cushion in a high-yield savings account.** The exception is if you already have 3+ months of expenses saved. In that case, put it on the loan.

## The numbers

**Your loan as-is:**
- Payment: about **$393/month**
- Interest remaining over 41 months: about **$1,910**

**If you put $5,000 on it now:**
- Balance drops to $9,200
- Your payment **stays $393/month**, because car loans don't re-amortize
- Paid off in about **26 months** instead of 41
- Interest drops to about $770, saving roughly **$1,150**

**If you keep it in savings at about 4%:**
- It earns roughly $500–550 over the same period (less after tax)
- Net cost of keeping the cushion: **about $600 total, or $14–15/month**

## Why I'd keep it

1. **Paying down the loan doesn't free up any monthly cash until it's gone.** Your daycare costs rise $250/month in January, and the loan still takes $393/month either way. The prepayment only helps 26 months from now.
2. **Cash is flexible and the loan isn't.** $5,000 covers the daycare increase for 20 months if your budget can't absorb it. It also covers a car repair or a gap in income. Once it's in the loan, you can't get it back.
3. **The insurance is cheap.** About $15/month buys you $5,000 of flexibility while your costs are going up.

## What I'd actually do

- Put the $5,000 in a HYSA now.
- Run January through March with the higher daycare cost and see if your budget handles the extra $250 without touching the cushion.
- If it does and you have other emergency savings, send most of the $5,000 to the loan in spring. Waiting a few months costs you about $40–50.
- If you'd have to dip into it, you'll be glad you kept it.

The 7.4% guaranteed return from prepaying is real. But the right time to lock in that return is after you know your new monthly budget works, not right before a cost increase.

Q25-C.text:
# Team Planning Meeting: Checklist and Budget

**14 staff · 8:30–12:30 · AUD 600 for catering and room · 2 vegan · 1 nut allergy**

## The key question: do you need to pay for the room?

Room hire is the main thing that changes the budget, so I've given two scenarios. All prices are rough estimates for an Australian capital city, GST-inclusive. Regional areas are often 15–25% cheaper and Sydney/Melbourne CBD can be higher.

### Scenario A: External room hire (morning tea only)

| Item | Estimate | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Meeting room, half day (holds 16–20) | $220–300 | Library, council, co-working or community rooms sit at the lower end. Hotels and CBD venues are often $350+. |
| Arrival tea/coffee (8:15–8:45) | $60–80 | About $5 per head, if the venue doesn't include it. |
| Morning tea (~10:15) | $180–220 | About $13–16 per head. |
| Delivery fee / minimum order surcharge | $0–40 | Check this, since many caterers charge it. |
| Contingency (~8–10%) | $50 | For extra drinks, AV fees or a late addition. |
| **Total** | **~$560–600** | |

**Tip:** Many venues sell a half-day package with the room, tea/coffee and morning tea for around $35–45 per head. For 14 people that's $490–630. Always ask for a package quote, because it's often cheaper than booking separately.

### Scenario B: Free in-house room (more food)

| Item | Estimate | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Room | $0 | |
| Arrival coffee, tea and light breakfast (pastries, fruit) | $100–130 | About $7–9 per head. |
| Morning tea | $180–210 | About $13–15 per head. |
| Working lunch at 12:30 to close the session | $250–300 | About $18–21 per head for wraps, salads and fruit. |
| Contingency | $30–50 | |
| **Total** | **~$560–600** | |

If you choose Scenario B, a short lunch at 12:30 is a good use of the budget. It gives people time to talk informally, which planning sessions benefit from. If people need to leave at 12:30, drop the lunch and upgrade to barista coffee or a fuller breakfast.

### Rule-of-thumb split

- **External room:** about 45% room, 45% catering, 10% buffer.
- **Free room:** about 85–90% catering, 10–15% buffer.

Keep at least $40–50 unallocated until the invoice arrives.

## Dietary requirements

**The simplest and safest option is to make the whole order nut-free.** This removes the risk of mix-ups at the shared table, and it costs nothing extra.

### Nut allergy
- [ ] **Ask the person privately and early** about the details. Is it peanuts, tree nuts or both? Is it anaphylactic? Do "may contain traces" items matter to them? Do they carry an adrenaline auto-injector?
- [ ] Ask whether they want anything arranged, such as letting the first aid officer know. Let them decide how much is shared with others.
- [ ] Tell the caterer in writing that the order must be nut-free, including peanuts, tree nuts, almond meal, nut oils, pesto, satay and praline.
- [ ] Ask the caterer how they handle cross-contact. Do they make nut products in the same kitchen? Australian food businesses must be able to give you allergen information when you ask.
- [ ] If the caterer can't guarantee nut-free, order the allergic person's food **separately packaged and labelled with their name**, or use a specialist allergy-friendly supplier.
- [ ] Check what people bring in themselves, such as shared snacks or muesli bars on the table.
- [ ] Know who your first aiders are and confirm the room has a first aid kit. Some workplaces keep a general-use adrenaline auto-injector.

### Vegan
- [ ] **Watch where vegan and nut-free overlap.** Many vegan foods rely on nuts: cashew "cheese", almond milk, nut-based slices, bliss balls and pesto. Make sure the vegan items are **also nut-free**.
- [ ] For plant milk, order **oat or soy milk, not almond**. One litre of oat milk is usually enough for 14 people.
- [ ] Order **4–5 vegan portions, not just 2**, because other people tend to eat them. Label them clearly, and ask the caterer to pack them separately if possible.
- [ ] Ask for at least one vegan item that is filling, not just fruit. Good options include savoury muffins, vegan banana bread, rice paper rolls or a hummus and vegetable box (check the hummus is nut-free).
- [ ] Ask the two vegan staff if they have preferences. Some people are also gluten-free or avoid particular items.

### Good options that suit everyone
- Seasonal fruit platter
- Nut-free vegan banana bread or muffins
- Rice paper rolls with a nut-free dipping sauce (satay is usually peanut-based)
- Vegetable sticks with hummus
- Scones with jam (add cream separately for non-vegans)
- Savoury pinwheels or mini quiches for non-vegans, labelled

## Room checklist

- [ ] **Capacity:** book a room that holds 16–20 people. A room for exactly 14 feels cramped for planning work.
- [ ] **Access time:** confirm you can get in from about **8:00** to set up. Many venues open at 8:30, which leaves no setup time.
- [ ] **Layout:** a U-shape or boardroom layout works for discussion. Cabaret-style round tables suit breakout group work.
- [ ] **AV:** screen or projector, HDMI/USB-C adaptors, a working clicker, and video call equipment if anyone joins remotely.
- [ ] **Planning tools:** whiteboards, flipcharts, markers that work, sticky notes, Blu Tack, and wall space for sticking things up.
- [ ] **Wi-Fi** login details and enough **power points** or power boards for laptops.
- [ ] **Breakout space** if you plan small-group sessions.
- [ ] **Catering space:** a separate table for food away from the work tables, and somewhere to keep milk cold.
- [ ] **Water:** jugs and glasses, or a water station.
- [ ] **Accessibility:** step-free access, accessible toilets, lifts. Ask staff about any needs.
- [ ] **Practical details:** temperature control, natural light, noise from next door.
- [ ] **Terms:** cancellation policy, deposit, what's included, cleaning or overtime fees if you run late.
- [ ] **Location:** transport and parking for staff.

## Catering checklist

- [ ] Get **2–3 quotes**. Confirm whether GST and delivery are included and check the minimum order.
- [ ] Confirm the **delivery time**: arrival drinks by 8:15 and morning tea by 10:00 for a 10:15 break. Ask whether they can deliver both at 8:15 and you hold the morning tea.
- [ ] Ask about **crockery and cups versus disposable** items, whether there is a pickup charge, and whether you need to provide a bin or clean up.
- [ ] Order for **14 people, not 16**. Catering portions are usually generous. The extra vegan portions are your buffer.
- [ ] Have a **clear label for each item** listing allergens and whether it is vegan.
- [ ] Have a **tea and coffee setup** with hot water, a range of teas, instant or pod coffee, dairy milk plus oat or soy milk, sugar, and spoons.
- [ ] Get a **written confirmation** of the order showing dietary requirements, and save it.

## Timeline

**2–3 weeks before**
- [ ] Confirm budget approval and the cost code.
- [ ] Decide between an in-house and external room, then book it.
- [ ] Send the calendar invite. Ask for dietary or accessibility needs to confirm what you already know and catch anything new.
- [ ] Speak privately to the person with the nut allergy.

**1–2 weeks before**
- [ ] Get catering quotes and place the order with dietary needs in writing.
- [ ] Confirm the agenda with the facilitator and plan the break times.
- [ ] Book any AV, video link or extra equipment.

**2–3 days before**
- [ ] Reconfirm numbers and delivery times with the caterer and venue. Many need final numbers 48–72 hours ahead.
- [ ] Send attendees the agenda, location, start time and Wi-Fi details.
- [ ] Prepare stationery and print agendas or materials.

**On the day**
- [ ] Arrive at 8:00 and check the room layout, AV, Wi-Fi and temperature.
- [ ] Check the catering on arrival against the order. Make sure the vegan and nut-free items are labelled and kept separate.
- [ ] Point the allergic and vegan staff to their food before others start eating.
- [ ] Keep track of time so morning tea happens when planned.

**Afterwards**
- [ ] Reconcile invoices against the budget.
- [ ] Return anything you hired or borrowed.
- [ ] Send a quick feedback question about the food and room for next time.

## Suggested running sheet

| Time | Activity |
|---|---|
| 8:00 | Set up and catering arrives |
| 8:15 | Arrival tea and coffee |
| 8:30 | Start |
| 10:15–10:35 | Morning tea (20 minutes) |
| 12:15 | Wrap-up and actions |
| 12:30 | Close, or working lunch in Scenario B |

Four hours is long for one block of work. Even with morning tea at about 10:15, add a short 5-minute stretch break around 11:30.

## Ways to make the budget go further

- Ask for half-day venue packages, which are often better value than booking room and food separately.
- Library, council and university rooms are often much cheaper than hotels. Some are free for community or not-for-profit use.
- Choosing one or two more substantial items is better than a large spread of small ones.
- Instant or pod coffee costs much less than barista coffee. A coffee cart is usually $250 or more for 14 people.
- Fresh fruit is cheap, suits everyone, and is safe for vegan and nut-free needs.

If you tell me your city, whether you have a free room, and whether you'd like to include lunch, I can narrow this to a single budget and suggest a sample catering order.

Q21-B.text:
# Monday to Friday Dinner Plan: 6 People, ₦45,000, Groundnut-Free, Under 40 Minutes

## Groundnut Safety

Groundnut can hide in a few places in Nigerian cooking, so these rules apply to every meal below:

- **Cooking oil:** "Vegetable oil" blends sometimes contain groundnut oil. Buy a bottle labelled **soybean oil** or **palm olein**. Avoid any label that says groundnut, peanut or arachis oil.
- **Grinding:** Market grinding machines often grind groundnut too. **Blend your tomatoes and pepper at home** and buy crayfish whole if you can. If you buy it ground, use a seller who doesn't grind groundnut.
- **Fried fish:** Don't buy fish already fried at the market. Fry it at home in your own oil.
- **Seasoning cubes and curry:** Check the allergen line on the pack before buying.
- **No suya, suya pepper (yaji) or kuli-kuli** this week.

## The Week at a Glance

| Day | Dinner | Cook time |
|---|---|---|
| Monday | Boiled yam with egg and tomato sauce | 30 min |
| Tuesday | Jollof spaghetti with boiled eggs | 30 min |
| Wednesday | White rice, tomato stew (double batch) and fried titus fish | 35–40 min |
| Thursday | Yam porridge (asaro) with ugwu and crayfish | 35 min |
| Friday | White rice, Wednesday's stew, chicken and fried plantain | 35–40 min |

Times assume a two-burner gas cooker and the cook starting at 7:00pm. Anyone at home before 7pm can peel, wash and chop to make it faster.

## Daily Method

### Monday: Boiled Yam and Egg Sauce
Uses 1 yam tuber, 12 eggs, about ¼ of the tomatoes and pepper, 1 onion, vegetable oil, seasoning and salt.
1. **7:00:** Peel and cut the yam into medium slices. Wash, add salt and boil (20–25 min).
2. **7:05:** Blend ¼ of the tomatoes and pepper. Slice 1 onion.
3. **7:10:** Fry the onion in 4 tablespoons of oil. Add the tomato blend, 1 cube and salt. Fry for 10 min.
4. **7:22:** Beat the 12 eggs, pour them into the sauce and stir gently for 3–4 min until set.
5. **7:30:** Drain the yam and serve.

### Tuesday: Jollof Spaghetti with Boiled Eggs
Uses 2 packs of spaghetti (1kg), 6 eggs, 2 sachets of tomato paste, about ¼ of the tomatoes and pepper, 1 onion, oil, seasoning, curry and thyme.
1. **7:00:** Boil the 6 eggs in one pot (10 min). Then cool, peel and halve them.
2. **7:00:** On the other burner, fry the onion in 5 tablespoons of oil. Add 2 paste sachets and fry for 3 min. Add the tomato blend and fry for 7 min.
3. **7:12:** Add about 1.2 litres of water, 2 cubes, curry, thyme and salt. Bring to the boil.
4. **7:15:** Break in the spaghetti and stir. Cover and cook on medium for 12–15 min, stirring now and then, until the water is absorbed.
5. **7:30:** Serve with the egg halves on top.

### Wednesday: White Rice, Tomato Stew and Fried Titus
Uses 1 derica of rice, the 2 titus fish, about ½ of the tomatoes and pepper, 2 sachets of tomato paste, 2 onions, oil, seasoning, curry, thyme and salt.

**Make double stew tonight. Half is for Friday.**
1. **7:00:** Wash the rice and boil it with salt (20 min until soft, then drain).
2. **7:00:** Cut the fish into 8 pieces, wash, and season with salt and 1 cube. Blend ½ of the tomatoes and pepper with 1 onion.
3. **7:05:** Heat ½ cup of oil and fry the fish, 4 pieces at a time, about 5 min per side. Remove the fish.
4. **7:20:** In the same oil, fry 1 sliced onion and 2 paste sachets for 3 min. Add the blend, 2 cubes, curry, thyme and salt.
5. **7:20–7:40:** Fry on medium until the oil floats on top, stirring so it doesn't burn. Serve with the rice and fish.
6. **After dinner:** Put half the stew in a covered bowl in the fridge. If there's no power, boil it well once on Thursday and again before Friday's dinner.

### Thursday: Yam Porridge with Ugwu
Uses the second yam tuber, the 2 bunches of ugwu, crayfish, palm oil, the remaining tomatoes and pepper, 1 onion, seasoning and salt.
1. **7:00:** Peel and cube the yam into small pieces so it cooks faster. Wash, then put it in a pot with water just covering it, plus salt and 1 cube.
2. **7:05:** While the yam cooks, slice the ugwu and onion and blend the remaining tomatoes and pepper.
3. **7:15:** Add the blend, onion, 3 tablespoons of crayfish and ⅓ of the palm oil. Cook for 10–12 min until the yam is soft. Mash a few pieces to thicken it.
4. **7:30:** Stir in the ugwu and cook for 3 min. Serve.

### Friday: White Rice, Stew, Chicken and Fried Plantain
Uses 1 derica of rice, 1kg of chicken, the 4 plantains, the saved stew, oil, seasoning, curry and thyme.

**On Thursday night,** move the chicken from the freezer to the fridge to thaw. Ask the seller to cut it into small pieces when you buy it.
1. **7:00:** Boil the chicken with ½ onion, 1 cube, curry, thyme and salt (18–20 min).
2. **7:00:** Wash the rice. Once the chicken is in, start the rice on the second burner (20 min).
3. **7:20:** Drain the chicken and save the stock. Fry the chicken in hot oil for 5–6 min until golden.
4. **7:27:** In the same oil, fry the 4 sliced plantains for about 3 min per side.
5. **7:35:** Heat the saved stew with a splash of chicken stock until it bubbles well. Serve with the rice, chicken and plantain.

## Shopping List

| # | Item | Quantity | Est. cost (₦) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Yam | 2 medium tubers | 7,000 |
| 2 | Eggs | 18 | 4,000 |
| 3 | Frozen chicken, cut small | 1kg | 6,000 |
| 4 | Titus (mackerel) fish | 2 fish, about 800g | 5,000 |
| 5 | Parboiled rice | 2 derica | 4,400 |
| 6 | Spaghetti | 2 × 500g packs | 2,400 |
| 7 | Plantain, slightly ripe | 4 fingers | 1,600 |
| 8 | Fresh tomatoes, tatashe and scotch bonnet | 1 mixed bag | 4,000 |
| 9 | Onions | 5 large | 1,200 |
| 10 | Tomato paste | 4 × 70g sachets | 1,200 |
| 11 | Soybean or palm olein oil (check label) | 1 litre | 3,200 |
| 12 | Palm oil | 50cl | 1,500 |
| 13 | Ugwu leaves | 2 bunches | 1,000 |
| 14 | Crayfish | 1 small cup | 500 |
| 15 | Seasoning cubes (check label) | 12 cubes | 600 |
| 16 | Curry and thyme | 1 sachet each | 400 |
| 17 | Salt | 1 small pack | 300 |
| | **Total** | | **44,300** |
| | **Left from ₦45,000** | | **700** |

## Buying and Storage Tips

- **Shop on Saturday or Sunday.** Yam, onions, rice and spaghetti keep fine all week.
- **Plantain:** Buy them yellow with a little green so they are ripe by Friday.
- **Tomatoes:** Use them early in the week, or blend everything on Sunday and keep it in the fridge.
- **Prices:** These are my estimates for a typical market. I can't check today's prices, and they vary by city and market. If your total runs over:
  1. Drop the titus and serve Wednesday's rice and stew with the leftover chicken stock flavour instead. This saves about ₦5,000.
  2. Or buy 3 plantains instead of 4.
- **If your son's allergy is severe,** make sure your other cooking utensils and grinder haven't been used for groundnut recently, and keep his usual allergy medicine handy as normal.

**Your loan now:** $14,200 at 7.4% over 41 months works out to about **$393/month**. If you just keep paying, you'll pay about **$1,914 in remaining interest**.

**If you put the $5,000 toward the loan:**

## Why I'd keep it

1. **Prepaying doesn't help your monthly budget until 2028.** Your real problem starting in January is $250 more going out every month. Paying down the loan leaves your $393 payment unchanged for 26 months, so it does nothing for that squeeze.
2. **$5,000 covers the daycare increase for 20 months** if you need time to rebalance your budget.
3. **Cash you've sent to the lender is gone.** If the car breaks, a job wobbles, or daycare costs rise again, you can't get it back without borrowing, probably at a worse rate than 7.4%.
4. **You can always prepay later. You can't un-prepay.** If six months from now the extra $250 fits in your budget and the $5,000 is untouched, send some of it to the loan then. You'll have given up only about $100 of interest savings for that flexibility.

## The one case where I'd flip

If you **already have 3+ months of expenses saved elsewhere** and this $5,000 would be extra, put it on the loan. A guaranteed 7.4% return beats any savings account.

## Also worth checking this month

It's mid-November, which is open enrollment for many employers. If your job offers a **Dependent Care FSA**, the limit rose to $7,500 for 2026. Paying daycare with pre-tax dollars could offset a large share of that $250/month increase, depending on your tax bracket. Check whether you also qualify for the Child and Dependent Care Credit, since you can't claim it on the same dollars you run through the FSA.

**Bottom line:** Put the $5,000 in a high-yield savings account, absorb the daycare increase for a few months, and revisit paying down the loan once your new budget proves stable.

Q27-B.text:
# Bathroom Budget: Can You Afford Heated Floors?

**Short answer:** Not with a safe buffer at the current numbers. With heated floors you'd have **CAD 400 left (about 3%)**. Bathroom renovations should carry a **10–15% contingency** for surprises behind walls and under floors. That's about **CAD 1,360–2,040** on a CAD 13,600 job. You're short roughly **CAD 960–1,640**.

Heated floors are still within reach. You need to close that gap first.

## The Numbers

| | Without heated floors | With heated floors |
|---|---|---|
| Labour + basic materials | 11,200 | 11,200 |
| Heated floors | 0 | 2,400 |
| **Project total** | **11,200** | **13,600** |
| Left from CAD 14,000 | 2,800 (20%) | 400 (2.9%) |
| 10% contingency needed | 1,120 | 1,360 |
| **Surplus / shortfall after 10% buffer** | **+1,680** | **−960** |

Without heated floors you're comfortably covered. With them, you're about CAD 960 short of a minimum safe buffer.

## Check This First: Is Tax Included in the Quote?

This could change everything. If the CAD 11,200 and CAD 2,400 are **before tax**, the tax on CAD 13,600 would be:

- **5% GST** (AB, BC, MB, QC, SK, territories): CAD 680, which leaves you **−280** before any buffer
- **13% HST** (ON): CAD 1,768, which puts you **CAD 1,368 over budget**
- **15% HST** (NB, NS, NL, PE): CAD 2,040, which puts you **CAD 1,640 over budget**

(QC, BC, SK and MB add provincial sales tax on top of GST in some cases, so ask him.)

**Ask the contractor in writing: "Does the 11,200 and 2,400 include tax?"**

## Other Costs to Budget For

**Things to confirm are in the CAD 2,400 heated-floor price:**
- **Thermostat**: a programmable one runs CAD 150–350 on its own.
- **Electrician and dedicated circuit**: most floor systems need their own GFCI-protected circuit, and a licensed electrician may need to install it. This can run CAD 300–800 if it's not included.
- **Electrical permit and inspection**: often CAD 100–250.

**Things to confirm are in "basic materials":**
- **Fixtures**: toilet, vanity, sink, faucet, shower valve and head, mirror, lighting, towel bars. If these aren't included, they can easily add CAD 1,500–4,000.
- **Tile allowance**: what price per square foot does the quote assume? Picking tile above that allowance costs extra.
- **Exhaust fan**: worth upgrading if yours is old or noisy. Moisture is what kills bathrooms.
- **Waste disposal and bin rental.**
- **Building/plumbing permit**, if your municipality requires one.

**Living without your only bathroom for 3 weeks (5 January to about 26 January):**
- Ask the contractor if he can **reconnect the toilet each evening** or keep it working for as long as possible. Many will if asked up front.
- Showering options: a gym day pass or short membership (about CAD 50–100 for the month), a friend or family member, or a portable toilet rental (about CAD 200–400 for 3 weeks, if allowed where you live).
- Worst case, a few hotel nights during the toughest stretch.
- **Set aside about CAD 150–400** for this.

**Delays:** Three weeks is the plan. In January, with possible holiday backlogs on materials and surprises once the old floor comes up, a 4–5 week reality is common. Plan your living arrangements with some slack.

## How to Get Heated Floors and Keep a Buffer

You need to find about **CAD 1,000–1,600** (more if tax isn't included). Options:

1. **Heat only the walking area.** Mats aren't installed under the tub, vanity or toilet anyway. Ask whether a smaller mat lowers the CAD 2,400.
2. **Choose cheaper tile and fixtures.** This is usually the easiest place to save CAD 500–1,500 without hurting quality.
3. **Ask for the detailed breakdown** of the CAD 11,200 and see whether anything can be value-engineered.
4. **Do demo or cleanup yourself**, if he agrees. This can save a few hundred dollars.
5. **Add a bit to the budget.** Raising it to about CAD 15,000 gives you heated floors plus a 10% buffer, as long as tax is included in the quote.

**One reason to prioritize heated floors now:** they can't be cheaply added later. You'd have to rip up the new tile. Fixtures, mirrors and lighting can be upgraded any time. If you must trade something off, give up a fancier vanity before you give up the floor.

## Questions to Send the Contractor

1. Are the CAD 11,200 and CAD 2,400 prices before or after tax?
2. Does the heated-floor price include the thermostat, electrical circuit, electrician and permit?
3. What exactly is covered by "basic materials"? Which fixtures, and what tile allowance per sq ft?
4. Who pulls permits, and are permit fees included?
5. Can the toilet be kept working, or reconnected overnight, during the job?
6. How do you handle surprises like rot or water damage? Will you get my approval in writing before doing extra work?
7. What's the payment schedule? (Avoid paying more than 10–25% up front.)

**Bottom line:** Heated floors are worth having in a Canadian January bathroom. At CAD 400 of leftover room, though, one rotten subfloor patch would put you over budget. Find about CAD 1,000 in savings or extra funds, confirm tax, and then go for it.

Q26-C.text:
# A Better Baking Plan for Weekdays and Saturdays

You have two opposite problems:

- **Weekdays:** You bake too much. About 15 loaves are wasted every day, roughly 75 a week.
- **Saturdays:** You bake too little. Selling out by 1pm means you're turning customers away for the rest of the day.

The fix for both is the same: **bake a fixed base amount in the morning, then decide on extra batches during the day based on how sales are actually going.** Your 20-loaf oven limit makes this easy, because each batch is a natural decision point.

---

## 1. What your numbers tell you

| | Baked | Left over | Actually sold |
|---|---|---|---|
| Weekday | 80 | ~15 | **~65** |
| Saturday | 120 | 0 (gone by 1pm) | **120+, true demand unknown** |

Weekday demand is about 65. Some days will be higher and some lower, which is why baking exactly 65 every day isn't the answer.

Saturday's real demand is hidden. You only know it's more than 120. If you're open until 4–5pm, you could be missing 20–50+ sales.

---

## 2. Weekday plan: 60 base + a flexible top-up (target ~65–70)

**Morning: 3 full batches (60 loaves).**
Time them so all three are out of the oven by opening, or the third shortly after. For example, if a batch takes about an hour from loading to cooling:

| Batch | Loaves | Into oven | Ready |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 20 | ~5:00 | opening |
| 2 | 20 | ~6:00 | opening / shortly after |
| 3 | 20 | ~7:00 | early morning |

**Late morning (~10:30–11:00): count what's left, then decide.**

| Loaves left on the shelf at ~11am | Top-up batch |
|---|---|
| Fewer than 20 | Full batch (20) |
| 20–30 | Half batch (~10) |
| More than 30 | Skip it |

This top-up comes out of the oven around midday, so your afternoon customers get fresh bread too.

**Expected result:** most days you'll bake 65–75, with leftovers dropping from ~15 to around 3–6. That's roughly **50 fewer loaves wasted per week.**

The thresholds above are starting guesses. After 2 weeks of tracking (see section 5) you'll know your typical "sold by 11am" figure and can adjust them.

---

## 3. Saturday plan: 120 base + 1–2 afternoon batches (try 140 first)

**Early morning: 6 batches (120 loaves)**, as you do now. Front-load them, since Saturday mornings are clearly busy.

**Add batch 7 (20 loaves), timed to come out around 11:30–12:00.**
That's just before your current sell-out point, so it covers the gap.

**Optional batch 8:** at about 12:30, if the shelves are already looking thin, bake one more batch (10 or 20) to cover the mid-afternoon.

How to adjust over the next few Saturdays:

| What happens | Next Saturday |
|---|---|
| Still sell out before closing | Add another batch (go to 150–160) |
| Sell out within the last hour or so | About right. Keep it. |
| 10+ left over at close | Drop back by 10 |

Increase in steps of 10–20, not all at once. Selling out an hour before closing is often fine. Some unmet demand is cheaper than heavy waste.

**Bonus option:** take Saturday pre-orders (e.g. "order by Friday 3pm"). Guaranteed sales are risk-free baking and help you see real demand.

---

## 4. How much to over-bake? It depends on your margin

A useful rule of thumb: compare what a leftover loaf costs you with what a missed sale costs you.

- **Cost of a leftover loaf** = ingredients + energy (say £1)
- **Cost of a missed sale** = lost profit (price − cost, say £4 − £1 = £3)

If a missed sale costs you more than a wasted loaf (common with bread), it's worth baking slightly above average demand. With the example numbers above, you'd accept running out on only about 1 day in 4. That's why the weekday target is about 65–70 rather than exactly 65.

If your margins are thin, lean lower. If they're healthy, a few leftover loaves a day is fine.

---

## 5. Track this for 2–3 weeks (takes 1 minute a day)

| Date | Day | Baked | Left at 11am | Left at close | Sold out at (time) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|

This will show you:

- **Differences between weekdays.** Monday and Friday are often very different. You may end up with "Mon 60, Fri 75" rather than one number for every weekday.
- **Your morning/afternoon split**, so you can fine-tune the 11am decision rule.
- **True Saturday demand**, once you stop selling out early.

Also watch for weather, holidays, local events, and pay weeks. These shift demand noticeably.

---

## 6. Use up the leftovers you still have

Even with a good plan, you'll have a few spare loaves some days:

- **Last-hour discount** (e.g. half price after 4pm)
- **Too Good To Go** or similar apps, which sell surprise bags of end-of-day stock
- **Day-old shelf** at a reduced price the next morning
- **Make other products:** croutons, breadcrumbs, bread pudding, toasties
- **Donate** to a food bank or shelter. Many will collect.

---

## Summary

| Day | Morning (by opening) | Decision point | Top-up | Typical total |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Mon–Fri | 3 batches (60) | ~11am stock check | 0, 10, or 20 | ~65–75 |
| Saturday | 6 batches (120) | ~11am / 12:30 | +20, maybe +10–20 more | ~140–160 |

If you tell me your **bake time per batch, opening hours, and price/cost per loaf**, I can turn this into an exact oven schedule and fine-tune the targets.
