# Recommendation: €50

**Why €50 works:**
- **It's a modest catch-up.** €5 is about 11% over 3 years, roughly 3.5% a year. That's in line with what most costs have done in that time, so it won't look like a grab.
- **It covers the rent.** The extra €300/month is €3,600/year. At €5 more per cut, you need about **720 cut-and-blow-drys a year, or about 14 a week**, to cover it. If you do more than that, you're also getting back some of what inflation has taken.
- **It's a round number.** Older clients often pay cash, and €50 is easy: one note, no change. €49 or €52 just feels fiddly.
- **Clients expect it.** After 3 years, most regulars expect a rise. A small one is far less risky than holding until you need a big jump.

If you're very busy and turning people away, you could justify €52–55. But with a loyal, older client base, €50 is the safe sweet spot.

# Timing tip
Your clients come every 6 weeks, so **put the notice up by early-to-mid November** (about now). That way every regular sees it at least once before January. Mention it in person too while you're doing their hair, something like "Just so you know, I'm going up a little in January." Hearing it from you in person is what keeps regulars loyal.

# Window notice

> **A Note to Our Lovely Clients**
>
> Thank you for your loyalty. Many of you have been with us for years, and it means the world.
>
> After three years without a price change, and with rising costs, our prices will be updated from **1st January 2027**.
>
> **Cut & Blow-Dry: €50**
>
> We'll keep giving you the same care and attention you've always had. If you have any questions, just ask. We're always happy to chat.
>
> With warm thanks,
> [Your name / Salon name]

**Optional sweetener:** add "Book before 31st December at current prices." That rewards regulars and fills your December diary.

# Your New Price: €50

I'd go to **€50 from 1 January 2027**. Here's why it's the right number:

- **It's fair after 3 years.** Prices have risen roughly 7–9% since you last increased yours. That alone puts you at about €48.50. Rounding to €50 is a modest step that also covers your extra costs.
- **It covers your rent.** Your rent went up €300 a month. An extra €5 per cut and blow-dry covers that with 60 appointments a month. With clients coming every 6 weeks, that's about 83 regulars. If you have more, you come out ahead. At €48 you'd need 100 appointments a month to cover the same €300.
- **It's an easy number.** Older clients often pay in cash. €50 is one note, simple to remember, and avoids fiddling with change.
- **The risk is smaller than it feels.** At €50, you could lose 1 in 10 clients and still take in the same money, while working fewer hours. In practice, loyal clients who've seen you every 6 weeks for years rarely leave over €5, especially after 3 years without a rise.

**Why not smaller, more frequent rises?** You could, but one clear rise now is less awkward than raising prices again next year. After this, a small €1–2 increase every year or two keeps things gentle.

# Window Notice

> **A Note to Our Lovely Clients**
>
> From **1st January 2027**, a cut and blow-dry will be **€50**.
>
> We haven't changed our prices in three years. Like everyone, our costs have gone up, and this small change helps us keep giving you the same care and attention you've always had.
>
> Thank you for your loyalty. It truly means the world to us, and we look forward to seeing you in the new year.

# Tips for Telling Your Regulars

1. **Put the notice up now.** Today is 17 November, so a regular on a 6-week cycle will see it at least once before January.
2. **Mention it in person.** At the end of their appointment, say something like: *"Just so you know, from January it'll be €50. It's the first change in three years."* Hearing it from you warmly matters more to regulars than any sign.
3. **Don't over-apologise.** Say it once, kindly and confidently, then move on. Too much apology makes clients think it's a bigger deal than it is.

Q44-C.text:
# Recommendation: Mango Sticky Rice

For a solo operator with 2 burners and a 2-hour rush, **mango sticky rice is the better choice by a wide margin.** The main reason is that all of its cooking happens before service, so it never competes with your pad thai for burners or for your hands. Fried chicken skewers would compete with your main dish at exactly the moment you can least afford it.

---

## 1. The Core Issue: Your Bottleneck During Rush

During 11:30–1:30, your limits are:

- **2 burners**, likely both running pad thai
- **One person** taking orders, cooking, plating, and handling payment
- **Ticket time**, the main thing that keeps your line moving

A good second dish should add revenue **without using any of those three during rush.**

| Factor | Mango Sticky Rice | Fried Chicken Skewers |
|---|---|---|
| Burner use during rush | **None** (cooked beforehand) | Ties up 1 burner continuously for hot oil |
| Your time per order | ~15–30 sec (grab and hand over) or ~1 min (slice mango, plate) | 5–8 min frying, plus monitoring |
| Effect on pad thai output | None | Could roughly halve it if a burner is lost |
| Raw meat handling mid-service | No | Yes (cross-contamination, glove and hand-washing changes) |
| Safety risk | Low | Hot oil in a small space, alone, during a rush |
| Extra equipment | Rice steamer or pot, containers | Fryer or deep pot, thermometer, oil storage and disposal |
| Permits and inspection | Usually simple | Deep frying is often restricted on carts or needs extra approval |
| Cleanup | Easy | Oil filtering and disposal, splatter |

## 2. Why Chicken Skewers Work Against You

**Burner conflict.** Frying needs oil held at about 350°F, which means a burner is committed to it the whole time. If one of your two burners becomes a fryer, your pad thai capacity during rush drops sharply. Pad thai is the item people came for, so that trade-off is likely to lose money.

**Attention split.** Frying is not something you can leave alone. Oil temperature drops when you add product, skewers need turning, and overcooked or undercooked chicken leads to complaints or food safety problems. Doing that while tossing a wok and taking payments, with no one else to help, is how orders get burned and lines stall.

**Food safety load.** Raw chicken means you have to:
- Keep it cold at 41°F or below until cooking
- Confirm it reaches 165°F inside
- Change gloves and wash hands between raw chicken and everything else

That is hard to do consistently when you're working alone and rushing.

**Possible cannibalization.** Some customers will order skewers *instead of* pad thai. That could lower your average ticket instead of raising it.

**Regulatory hurdles.** Many jurisdictions limit open deep frying on push carts, or require fire suppression or a separate permit. Check with your health and fire departments before buying anything.

## 3. Why Mango Sticky Rice Fits

**All the work is done ahead of time:**
1. **The night before:** soak the glutinous rice for 4–8 hours or overnight.
2. **Morning, before service:** steam it for 25–30 minutes. Use your burners now, while they're free. Mix in the warm sweetened coconut milk and let it absorb.
3. **Also before service:** make the salty-sweet coconut topping sauce and pre-portion it.
4. **During rush:** slice the mango and assemble, or serve fully pre-packed clamshells.

**It's an add-on, not a replacement.** It's a dessert, so it raises your average ticket instead of taking orders away from pad thai. A line like *"Add mango sticky rice for $6?"* at checkout is an easy upsell.

**Good margins.** Rough numbers per portion:
- Glutinous rice: about $0.25–0.40
- Coconut milk and sugar: about $0.50–0.80
- Mango (half to one, depending on size and season): about $0.75–2.00
- Container and spoon: about $0.25–0.40
- **Total cost: roughly $2–3.50. Sells for about $7–9 at many carts.**

Check your own supplier prices, but the margin is usually healthy.

**It fills a gap in your menu.** You currently have only a savory hot item. Adding a sweet, cool item appeals to groups, people who want a treat, and people coming back for a second purchase.

**It helps your brand.** Pad thai plus mango sticky rice reads as a coherent Thai street food menu. Fried chicken skewers fit less clearly.

## 4. Risks and How to Handle Them

**Mango supply and price.** It's November, which is outside the main Mexican mango season, so imports from places like Peru, Ecuador, or Brazil are common and quality and price vary. Honey or Ataulfo mangoes are the best for this dish.
- Buy a few days ahead so they ripen properly.
- Build a price that tolerates mango cost swings.
- Have a fallback, such as "sticky rice with coconut cream" or a seasonal fruit, if good mangoes aren't available that day.

**Holding the rice safely and keeping its texture.**
- Refrigerated sticky rice turns hard and chalky, so it's best held at room temperature.
- Cooked rice is a time and temperature controlled food. Many health departments allow "time as a public health control," often up to 4 hours unrefrigerated, with logged times and discarding afterward.
- Confirm the rules with your local inspector.
- Make only what you expect to sell during service and toss leftovers. Don't hold it over to the next day.
- Keep the coconut sauce chilled until serving.

**Lower dessert demand at lunch.** Some people won't want dessert at noon.
- Present it as a grab-and-go treat or something to save for later.
- Bundle it, for example "pad thai + mango sticky rice for $X."
- Keep it visible on the cart. Seeing the bright mango sells it.

**Waste.**
- Start with a small batch, around 15–20 portions, and adjust based on sales.

## 5. How to Test It (2–3 Weeks)

1. **Start small:** 15–20 portions a day.
2. **Pre-pack most of them** so serving takes seconds.
3. **Upsell every customer** at payment.
4. **Track each day:**
   - Portions sold, and the time you sell out if you do
   - **Attach rate:** desserts sold ÷ pad thai orders. Around 15–25% is a solid result.
   - Whether your line moves more slowly
   - Waste, meaning portions thrown out
5. **Adjust** price, portion size, and batch quantity based on those numbers.

## 6. When Chicken Skewers Would Make Sense

Skewers could work later if your situation changes:

- **You get a third heat source,** such as a small charcoal grill kept only for skewers, and permits allow it. Grilling is also simpler than frying.
- **You hire a helper** for rush.
- **You want to reach customers who don't want noodles,** and you have capacity to spare.

Even then, grilled marinated skewers (Thai-style gai yang or moo ping) would usually suit a cart better than fried ones.

---

## Bottom Line

With 2 burners, no help, and a 2-hour rush, the best second dish is one you cook *before* rush and only hand over *during* it. Mango sticky rice does exactly that. It raises your average ticket, has good margins, fits your Thai menu, and leaves both burners for pad thai. Fried chicken skewers would take away the burner and the attention your main dish depends on.

Two things could change this advice: whether your local rules allow frying on your cart at all, and whether you already batch-cook pad thai or make each order to order. Tell me those, along with your current pad thai price, and I can help you work out pricing and a combo deal.

Q45-A.text:
# Family Dinner Plan: 18 Guests (Thursday to Saturday)

I've assumed **dinner at 7pm Saturday** and a North Indian-style menu. If you already have dishes in mind, tell me and I'll rework the timeline around them.

## The Menu

**(VG) = vegan.** Making the dal and chana vegan for everyone means fewer pots and no separate cooking.

| Dish | Vegan? | Made | Rough quantity for 18 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Lamb curry (rogan josh or similar) | No | Friday | 3.5kg boneless or 4.5kg on the bone |
| Palak paneer | No | Sauce Friday, paneer Saturday | 1kg paneer, 1.5kg spinach |
| Chana masala, cooked in oil | VG | Friday | 6 × 400g tins chickpeas |
| Tarka dal, oil tarka instead of ghee | VG | Friday | 750g dry lentils |
| Roasted aloo gobi | VG | Saturday (oven) | 3 cauliflowers, 1.5kg potatoes |
| Jeera or pilau rice | VG | Saturday (cook fresh) | 1.4kg dry basmati |
| Chapatis (shop-bought, check label) and papadums | VG | Bought | 40 chapatis |
| Naan | No (usually has milk) | Bought | 18 to 20 |
| Kachumber salad | VG | Saturday | |
| Raita | No | Saturday morning | 1kg yoghurt |
| Mint and tamarind chutneys (no yoghurt) | VG | Thursday | |
| Carrot halwa made with oil and oat or coconut milk | VG | Thursday | 2kg carrots |

## Thursday: Prep Day

**Morning or early afternoon**
- **Check your fridge space.** You'll need room for 4 to 5 big pots or tubs by Friday night. Clear a shelf now.
- Finish any shopping. **Check labels on chapatis, papadums and curry pastes** for milk, butter or ghee.

**Afternoon (about 2 to 3 hours)**
- **Ring 1:** Fry a big batch of onions, about 3kg, slowly until golden. This is the base for the lamb, chana and spinach. It's the most time-consuming job, so getting it done today saves hours. Cool it and split it into 3 tubs.
- **Ring 2:** Make the carrot halwa. It keeps 4 days in the fridge and tastes better after resting.
- Blend a large jar of ginger-garlic paste.
- Make the mint and tamarind chutneys.

**Evening**
- Marinate the lamb and refrigerate it overnight.
- If you're using dried chickpeas instead of tins, soak them now.

## Friday: Main Cooking Day (about 4 to 5 hours)

Use all 4 rings in a staggered way:

| Time | Ring 1 | Ring 2 | Ring 3 | Ring 4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 10:00 | Start lamb curry (2 to 2.5 hrs) | | | |
| 10:30 | | Lentils boiling | | |
| 11:00 | | | Chana masala (about 45 min) | |
| 11:30 | | Dal finished. Do the oil tarka in a small pan | | |
| 12:00 | | | Chana done, start cooling | Spinach sauce for palak (no paneer yet) |
| 12:30 | Lamb done by 12:30 to 1pm | | | Spinach done, cool |

**Important food safety point:** cool each dish quickly. Spread it into shallow containers or sit the pot in a sink of cold water, and get it in the fridge **within 2 hours**. Large pots of curry stay warm for a long time if left on the hob.

**Afternoon**
- Lay the table, or at least count out plates, cutlery and serving dishes. You'll need about 10 serving dishes.
- **Label the vegan serving spoons** (a ribbon or coloured clip works), so nobody moves the dal spoon into the raita.

## Saturday: Assembly Day

**Morning (relaxed)**
- Make the raita and refrigerate it.
- Chop the kachumber vegetables but **don't dress them yet**.
- Cut the cauliflower and potatoes and toss them in oil and spices.
- Cube the paneer.

**Afternoon: oven schedule (one tray at a time)**

| Time | Oven (about 210°C / 190°C fan) |
|---|---|
| 3:30 to 4:15 | Aloo gobi, batch 1 |
| 4:15 to 5:00 | Aloo gobi, batch 2. Combine with batch 1 in a covered dish |
| 6:30 to 6:45 | Turn the oven down. Briefly re-crisp the aloo gobi, then warm naans and chapatis wrapped in foil |

**Hob schedule**

| Time | What to do |
|---|---|
| 5:30 | **Rice** on 1 ring. Once cooked, keep the lid on and wrap the pot in a towel. It stays hot for over an hour. **Cook rice fresh today, not ahead**, because reheated rice is a food-poisoning risk. |
| 5:45 | Take the curries out of the fridge. |
| 6:00 | **Ring 1:** lamb. **Ring 2:** chana. **Ring 3:** dal (add a splash of water, since it thickens overnight). **Ring 4:** spinach sauce. Reheat gently and stir often. |
| 6:30 | Add the paneer to the spinach. Rice comes off its ring by now. |
| 6:45 | Check every curry is **piping hot all the way through**. Dress the kachumber. Put out the chutneys and raita. |
| 6:50 | Fry the papadums, or microwave them. |
| 7:00 | Serve. |

**Dessert:** take the halwa out at the start of dinner and warm it in the microwave or on a ring once the curries are served.

## Tips for Hosting 18

- **Hidden dairy** is the main vegan trap: butter in naan, cream stirred into curry "for richness," and yoghurt in chutneys. Keep the vegan dishes completely dairy-free and put them at one end of the table.
- **Recruit a helper** for 6 to 7pm on Saturday to do drinks, papadums and carrying dishes out.
- If you own a **slow cooker or rice cooker**, use it on Saturday. It frees up a ring and takes the pressure off.

I can also give you a combined shopping list for this menu, or rework the timeline for a different dinner time or different dishes.

Q48-C.text:
# Route Choice and Start Time for Your April Club Ride

**Short answer:** Choose **Route B (60 km, hilly)**, rolling out at **9:30 am**, as long as the hills are moderate. A fair test is total climbing under about 700 m and no long stretches steeper than about 8%. If the hills are steeper than that, choose **Route A** and roll out at **8:30 am**. Either way, aim to be back by **2:00–2:15 pm**, not 3:00.

The reasoning, timings and logistics are below.

---

## 1. The date

The next first Sunday of April is **Sunday, 4 April 2027**. Some things to know about that day:

- **Easter Sunday is 28 March 2027**, so 4 April falls in many school holiday periods. Expect busier roads near parks, coasts and tourist spots, and busier cafés. Book a café stop ahead.
- **Daylight saving has started** in both North America and Europe by then. Mornings are lighter, but early April starts are often cold. Depending on where you are, 8 am temperatures can be 3–8 °C even on a nice day.
- Check whether any part of either route is affected by Easter events, markets or roadworks.

---

## 2. Realistic timings

The key point is that **ride time is much more than distance divided by speed**. With 24 riders, regrouping, a café stop, toilet breaks and the odd puncture add a lot of time.

**Assumptions** for a mixed-ability social club ride:
- Flat moving average: 18–21 km/h
- Hilly moving average: 15–17 km/h
- These can be slower if the group is more casual or it's windy. Adjust if you know your club's normal pace.

| | **Route A (85 km, flat)** | **Route B (60 km, hilly)** |
|---|---|---|
| Moving time | 4h05 – 4h45 | 3h30 – 4h00 |
| Café stop | 35–45 min | 35–45 min |
| Regroups / comfort breaks | ~15–20 min | ~20–25 min (regroup at hill tops) |
| Mechanical / contingency | ~15 min | ~15 min |
| **Total elapsed** | **~5h15 – 6h00** | **~4h30 – 5h00** |
| Roll-out for a ~2:15 pm return | **~8:15–8:30 am** | **~9:15–9:30 am** |

**Why aim for 2:15 pm and not 3:00?** A group of 24 almost always runs later than planned. A couple of punctures, a slow café, a headwind or one rider having a bad day can easily add 30–45 minutes. Also, if people want to have a drink, eat or chat at the clubhouse after the ride, you need time before it closes.

---

## 3. Why Route B is the better default

**It fits the 3 pm deadline more comfortably.** Route A takes 5–6 hours in total, so it needs an early start and still leaves little margin. If anything goes wrong on an 85 km ride, you have few ways to recover the time. Route B has about an hour more slack.

**It allows a later, warmer start.** On an April morning, a 9:30 start instead of 8:15–8:30 often means several degrees warmer. That matters for comfort, stiff joints and how pleasant the ride feels.

**Less time in the saddle.** For many riders, especially older or less regular ones, four to six hours of continuous riding is tiring. Saddle soreness, neck and hand fatigue, and the need to eat and drink all build up. Riding 85 km is a big day for a casual group, even when it's flat.

**Moderate hills often feel easier than they look on paper.** As a rough guide, 60 km with modest climbing is about as hard as a 70–75 km flat ride. That is still less than Route A.

---

## 4. When Route A is the better choice

Choose Route A instead if any of these apply:

- **Route B has steep or long climbs.** Watch for sustained gradients above about 8–10%, or total climbing well above 800–1,000 m. Steep hills are where mixed groups struggle most. People with knee problems or heart conditions, and riders with less effective gearing, can find them hard or unsafe. They also spread the group out badly.
- **Route B's descents are technical or on busy roads.** Fast, twisty or poorly surfaced descents are a bigger crash risk than the climbs, especially for nervous riders.
- **Your club often rides 70–90 km.** If so, flat distance is familiar and Route A is very manageable.
- **Keeping everyone together is the top priority.** Flat roads keep a group tight. Riders can draft, chat, and nobody gets dropped. Hills split groups whatever you do.

**Weather can change the answer.** On a flat, exposed route, a strong headwind can make 85 km much harder than the hilly route. If you go with Route A, plan it so you ride **into the wind on the way out** and have it behind you on the way home, when people are tired.

---

## 5. A word on the over-60s

Being over 60 says less about cycling ability than you might think. Many riders in their 60s and 70s are among the strongest in any club. What matters more is:

- How often each person rides
- The longest distance they've done recently
- Any knee, back or heart issues
- Whether some members ride **e-bikes**. These flatten hills a lot, but check that batteries will last.

It's worth a quick poll in your club chat: *"Would you prefer 85 km flat or 60 km with some hills?"* Also ask a few members privately whether they'd be comfortable with each option. People are often more honest one-to-one.

---

## 6. A third option: split the group

24 riders is too many to ride safely as one bunch on public roads. Many clubs and national cycling bodies recommend groups of about 8–12. You'll probably split into two or three groups anyway, so you could use that:

- **Group 1 (steadier):** Route B, rolling out at 9:30
- **Group 2 (stronger, or riders who prefer flat):** Route A, rolling out at 8:30
- Both groups aim to finish around 2:00–2:15 pm at the clubhouse.

This way everyone gets the ride that suits them, and you all finish together.

---

## 7. Practical checklist

**Before the day**
- Get the **elevation profile** for Route B from Strava, Komoot, RideWithGPS or similar. Check the total climbing and the steepest sections.
- If possible, ride or drive the route a week or two beforehand. Look for potholes, roadworks and closed cafés.
- Book the café stop. With 24 people in Easter holidays, this is essential. Ideally the stop should be roughly 55–65% of the way round.
- Mark **bail-out points or shortcuts** where anyone struggling can cut the ride short, and know where the nearest railway stations are.
- Share the GPX file and a **written schedule** with planned times at each regroup point, so leaders can tell if they're running late.

**On the day**
- Ask people to arrive 20–30 minutes before roll-out for a safety briefing. Leave on time.
- Have a **leader and a back marker (sweep)** for each group, with phones and each other's numbers.
- Regroup at the **tops of climbs** and at tricky junctions.
- Set a "decision time." For example: if a group hasn't reached the café by a certain time, take the shortcut home.
- Ask riders to bring layers (gilet, arm warmers, gloves) for a cold start, a spare tube, food, two bottles, and emergency contact details.
- Make sure someone in each group carries a basic first-aid kit. If possible, have a support car or a member on call with a car or van to collect anyone who needs to stop.
- Check the forecast for temperature, rain and especially **wind direction** 48 hours before, and confirm the route then.

---

## Summary

| | Recommendation |
|---|---|
| **Default choice** | **Route B**, roll-out **9:30 am** (meet 9:00), back ~2:00–2:15 pm |
| **If Route B's hills are steep or technical** | **Route A**, roll-out **8:30 am** (meet 8:00), back ~2:00–2:30 pm |
| **Best of both** | Split into groups, with both routes finishing around the same time |
| **Must-do** | Check Route B's elevation profile and poll members on what they'd prefer |

If you can share Route B's total climbing and steepest gradients, or your club's usual average speed, I can firm up the recommendation and work out a detailed timed schedule with the café stop and regroup points.

Q51-A.text:
Forty years in a farmhouse into a two-bed bungalow with no attic or garage is a big change, but you have about 14 weeks. That's enough time if you start now and work in order.

## The golden rule

**Keep only what has a place in the bungalow.** Before anything else, get the floor plan or measure the rooms, including wardrobes, kitchen cupboards and wall space. Sketch where your furniture will go. If an item doesn't fit on that plan, it isn't coming, however good it is. This one step settles most of the arguments before they start.

## Keep, sell or give away

**Keep**
- Furniture that fits the plan and that you actually use (your bed, favourite chairs, the good table if it fits)
- Everyday kitchen things. A two-bed kitchen holds roughly a third of a farmhouse kitchen, so keep one set of good dishes and pots, not three.
- Clothes you've worn in the past year
- Important papers: deeds, wills, pensions, medical records. Keep about 6 years of tax and financial records. Older ones can be shredded.
- A curated set of sentimental items. Pick a box each, say, rather than keeping everything.

**Sell**
- Farm machinery, tools and equipment: DoneDeal, local marts, or a clearance auction if there's a lot of it
- Good furniture and antiques: a local auctioneer can value and take a whole lot at once, which saves selling piece by piece
- Smaller items: Adverts.ie, DoneDeal, local Facebook buy-and-sell groups

Be realistic about prices. Brown furniture sells cheaply these days. If something won't sell within a couple of weeks, move it to "give away."

**Give away**
- **Family first.** Tell Declan and any other children, grandchildren or relatives to claim what they want by a set date, say mid-December, and to collect it themselves.
- **Charities.** St Vincent de Paul and some others collect furniture free, so it doesn't use Declan's van. Charity shops take clothes, books and bric-a-brac.
- Facebook "free to collect" groups and Freecycle for things charities won't take
- Clare County Council recycling centres, or a skip, for the rest

**Sentimental items**
- Photos and letters can be scanned. Grandchildren are often glad to help with this.
- Take a photo of a much-loved item before letting it go. It keeps the memory without taking up the space.

## Timeline

| When | Focus |
|---|---|
| **Late Nov** | Get the floor plan and mark what's coming. Tell family the claim deadline. Book an auctioneer to look at furniture and farm items. |
| **Dec** | Clear the sheds, outbuildings and attic first. They're hardest and coldest, so better done before January. List items for sale. Family collect their claims. |
| **Early Jan** | Work room by room, least-used rooms first. Book charity collections. Book a skip if needed. |
| **Late Jan – mid Feb** | Pack everything that's coming, labelling each box with its room in the *bungalow*. Sell or donate the last items. |
| **Final week** | Pack essentials and do the final clean. |

## Declan's two weekends

Don't use Declan's van for donations or dump runs. Charities collect, and a skip or trailer handles waste. Save his time for the jobs only he can do.

**Weekend 1 (mid-December): heavy lifting and clearing**
- Bring heavy or awkward items down from the attic and out of the sheds so you can sort them
- Take away anything he or his siblings are keeping
- Do one or two runs to the recycling centre if there's a lot of bulky waste
- Move pieces the two of you shouldn't lift into one "going" room and one "leaving" room

**Weekend 2 (the move, end of February): the actual move**
- Packing should be completely finished beforehand, so he's only loading and driving
- Load the big furniture first, then boxes, with bed and kitchen essentials last on so they come off first
- Set up your bed the first night

**Consider hiring help for one piece of the move.** A local man-with-a-van or small removal firm for half a day could take the largest furniture, so Declan's van handles everything else. It also gives you a backup if the weather turns or one trip isn't enough.

## Questions that would sharpen this plan

1. How far is the farmhouse from Ennis? It decides how many van runs fit in a day.
2. Will you have keys to the bungalow before the move? If so, Weekend 1 could move a first load of non-essentials across.
3. Is there farm machinery or livestock equipment to sell? That may need its own plan.
4. Are there other children or family who will want things?

Tell me a bit more and I can turn this into a week-by-week checklist you can print and stick on the fridge.

Q52-A.text:
# Short answer

**You can't comfortably afford JLT on 2 cheques with AED 45,000. Al Barsha on 4 cheques is affordable and leaves you a buffer.** JLT could work if the landlord accepts 4 cheques.

## Upfront cost estimate

These are typical Dubai move-in costs. Confirm the exact figures with the agent.

| Item | JLT (85k, 2 cheques) | Al Barsha (72k, 4 cheques) |
|---|---|---|
| First rent cheque | 42,500 | 18,000 |
| Security deposit (~5%, unfurnished) | 4,250 | 3,600 |
| Agency fee (5% + 5% VAT) | 4,463 | 3,780 |
| Ejari registration | ~220 | ~220 |
| DEWA deposit + connection | ~2,130 | ~2,130 |
| Chiller/AC deposit (often applies in JLT) | ~1,000–2,000 | Often none (check) |
| Moving, internet, basics | ~2,000 | ~2,000 |
| **Total** | **~56,500–57,500** | **~29,700** |
| **Left from your 45k** | **About −12,000** | **About +15,000** |

**Al Barsha caveat:** you'll pay AED 18,000 every 3 months. That means setting aside about AED 6,000 a month for rent. With 4 cheques, the next payment comes around quickly.

## Commute to Media City

Both are close, so commuting shouldn't decide this.
- **JLT:** a few Red Line stops to Dubai Internet City station, then a short walk or tram. Roughly 10–15 minutes. A taxi is about AED 20–30.
- **Al Barsha 1** (near Mall of the Emirates): metro from MoE station to Internet City. Roughly 15 minutes. A taxi is about AED 25–35.
- **Barsha Heights (Tecom):** if the flat is here, it's essentially next door to Media City and may be walkable.
- Monthly transport cost will be similar for both, probably within AED 100–200 of each other.

## Recommendation

1. **Al Barsha is the sensible choice.** It saves AED 13,000 a year (about AED 1,080 a month), the commute is comparable, and you keep around AED 15,000 as an emergency fund.
2. **If you prefer JLT** (lifestyle, the lake, being nearer the Marina), ask for **4 cheques**. Some landlords will agree, sometimes at slightly higher rent. Upfront would then be about AED 35,000–36,000. That's doable, but your buffer would shrink to about AED 9,000–10,000, which is thin.
3. **Before signing either one,** ask:
   - Is it chiller-free, or is AC billed separately? Separate AC billing can add AED 300–800 a month in summer.
   - Is the agency fee negotiable?
   - Is the deposit 5% or 10%? Furnished flats are usually 10%.

If you share your monthly salary, I can check whether the ongoing rent fits the common guideline of keeping rent at or below about 30–35% of income.

Q50-C.text:
# Raising Your Cut & Blow-Dry Price in January

## Recommendation: €50

This is a modest, fair increase that most regulars will accept without a second thought.

**It's justified.** You haven't raised prices in 3 years. Eurozone inflation over that time adds up to roughly 10% (about 5.4% in 2023, 2.4% in 2024, 2.1% in 2025). Even at €50 you're only catching up, not getting ahead. In real terms, your €45 is now worth about €41.

**It covers your rent.** Divide the €300 increase by the number of cut & blow-dries you do each month:

| Cut & blow-dries per month | Extra needed per appointment |
|---|---|
| 60 | €5.00 |
| 80 | €3.75 |
| 100 | €3.00 |
| 120 | €2.50 |

A €5 increase covers the rent for most salons. That's before counting your other services, and before other rising costs like products, electricity and insurance.

**It's easy for clients.** A round €50 is simple to remember and simple to pay in cash, which matters for many older clients. €49 looks like a supermarket trick, and €52 feels fiddly.

**The risk is small.** At €50, you could lose 1 in 10 clients and still take in the same money while working fewer hours. In practice, a €5 rise after 3 years rarely loses more than a client or two. Your regulars come for you, the chat and the routine, not to save €5 every six weeks.

**When €52–55 might make sense instead:**
- Local salons of a similar standard already charge more.
- You're fully booked and turning people away.
- You've taken on other big cost increases.

A quick check of 3–4 nearby salons' price lists will tell you where you sit. If you're still the cheapest in the area at €50, you have room to go a bit higher.

## Don't forget the rest of your price list

Raising only the cut & blow-dry leaves the rest of your list behind. Apply a similar increase of roughly 10% to your other services, rounding to clean numbers. For example:
- Wash & set: €30 → €33
- Colour: €60 → €66

It's better to do everything once, in one announcement, than to raise prices piece by piece over the year.

## Timing: put the notice up now

Your clients come every 6 weeks, so a notice posted this week (mid-November) means **every regular sees it at least once before January**. Nobody should be surprised at the till.

- **Effective date:** a specific date reads better than "January." Pick something like **Monday 5 January 2026**.
- **Tell people in person too.** This matters more than the window sign. A friendly word while they pay works well (scripts below).
- **Honour existing commitments.** Gift vouchers and pre-paid appointments should be honoured at the old price.
- **Update everything at the same time:** the price list on the wall, any online booking page, and your Facebook or Google listing.

### An optional loyalty gesture

If you want to soften it for your regulars, you could say: *"Any appointments booked before 31 December stay at €45, even if they fall in January."*

This rewards loyalty, fills your January diary (often a quiet month), and makes the change feel generous. Keep it time-limited, though. Avoid offering a permanent "old price for existing clients," because it's very hard to undo.

## Window notice options

The tone should be warm, brief and confident: thank people, state the change clearly, and don't over-apologise.

### Option 1: Warm and simple (my pick)

> **A note to our lovely clients**
>
> Thank you for your loyalty. Many of you have been with us for years, and it means the world.
>
> After three years without a price change, our prices will be updated from **Monday 5 January 2026**.
> A cut & blow-dry will be **€50**.
>
> We'll keep giving you the same care, the same chat and the same warm welcome.
> If you have any questions, just ask. We're always happy to talk.
>
> *With thanks, [Your name]*

### Option 2: Mentions costs, gently

> **Price update from 5 January 2026**
>
> We've kept our prices the same for three years, but rising costs, including our rent, mean a small change is needed to keep the salon going.
>
> From **Monday 5 January**, a cut & blow-dry will be **€50**.
> Full updated price list available inside.
>
> Thank you for your continued support. We look forward to seeing you in the new year.

### Option 3: With the loyalty offer

> **Thank you for your loyalty**
>
> From **Monday 5 January 2026**, a cut & blow-dry will be **€50**, our first price change in three years.
>
> **Book before 31 December and your appointment stays at €45**, even if it's in January.
>
> Thank you for being part of our salon.

**Presentation tips:**
- Print it large and clear: at least 16–18pt for the main text, with the price and date in bold. That's easier for older eyes.
- Put a copy by the till as well as in the window.

## What to say in person

Many clients won't read the window. A quick friendly line at the till works better than any sign:

> *"Just to let you know, Mary, I'm putting my prices up a little in January, the first time in three years. A cut and blow-dry will be €50. If you'd like to book your next one before Christmas, I'll keep it at €45 for you."*

If someone grumbles:

> *"I know, nobody likes prices going up. I held off as long as I could, but my rent's gone up a lot. I really appreciate you coming to me."*

Then move on. Don't over-explain or apologise repeatedly, because that invites haggling. Most people simply nod.

## For the future

Rather than waiting another 3 years and having to make a bigger jump, plan a **small review every year**, around €1–2 each January. Clients barely notice small regular increases, and you won't fall behind your costs again.

## Summary

| Decision | Recommendation |
|---|---|
| New price | **€50** (about 11%, in line with 3 years of inflation) |
| Other services | Raise by about 10%, rounded to clean numbers |
| Notice goes up | **This week** |
| Effective date | **Monday 5 January 2026** |
| Loyalty sweetener (optional) | Book before 31 Dec, keep €45 |
| Communication | Window sign + sign by till + a friendly word in person |
| Going forward | Small annual review each January |

If you'd like, tell me your other services and current prices and I'll draft a full updated price list to match.

## Upfront cost on move-in day

- **Furnished flat:** the deposit is often 10% instead of 5%, which makes the gap bigger.

## Commute to Media City without a car

Both areas sit on the Red Line, so the commute won't decide this.

- Metro: DMCC station to Dubai Internet City is a few stops, about 5–10 minutes, then a short walk or the tram to Media City.

## Recommendation

**Take Al Barsha**, as long as the flat is within a reasonable walk of Mall of the Emirates or Sharaf DG metro station. You can afford it, it leaves you a cash buffer, and paying in 4 cheques means smaller amounts at a time. You save AED 13,000 a year and add only about 5–10 minutes to your commute.

**JLT only works if** you get the landlord to accept 4 cheques. That would make the first cheque about 21,250 and the total upfront roughly 32,300. Landlords sometimes agree but may add 2–5% to the rent. Even so, Al Barsha stays cheaper every year.

Q54-A.text:
# Soda Taper Plan: Now Through January 31

You have about 11 weeks, which is plenty of time to do this gently.

**Why tea helps:** A can of cola has about 35–45 mg of caffeine. A cup of black tea has about 40–50 mg. If you swap one soda for one black tea, your caffeine stays about the same, so you can drop the soda without the withdrawal headaches. Once the soda is gone, you can decide whether to cut back on caffeine too.

## Phase 1: Swap soda for tea (Nov 17 – Dec 31)

Replace one can at a time and hold each step for a week or two before the next.

| Dates | Soda | Replace with |
|---|---|---|
| Nov 17 – Nov 30 | 3 cans | 1 black tea |
| Dec 1 – Dec 14 | 2 cans | 2 black teas |
| Dec 15 – Dec 31 | 1 can | 3 black teas |
| **Jan 1 onward** | **0 cans** | 4 teas, or fewer (see Phase 2) |

Tips for this phase:
- **Drop your least important soda first.** Keep the one you love most, often the afternoon slump can, for last.
- **Thanksgiving and the holidays fall during "hold" periods.** You don't have to make a hard change during a busy week. If a week goes badly, just repeat that step.
- **Make tea that feels like a treat.** Iced black tea, chai, Earl Grey, or a cold brew bottle kept in the office fridge all work well. You can add a little honey or sugar at first and use less over time.
- **Use sparkling water for the fizz and the habit.** Many people miss the cold, fizzy can as much as the sugar. Keep flavored sparkling water at your desk. A splash of juice or a squeeze of lime in plain sparkling water makes it feel closer to soda.

## Phase 2: Optional caffeine reduction (January)

If you only wanted to quit soda, you're done. Keeping 2–4 cups of tea a day is moderate caffeine for most adults.

If you also want less caffeine, reduce slowly, about one cup's worth each week:
- **Week of Jan 4:** Change one black tea to green tea, which has about half the caffeine.
- **Week of Jan 11:** Change another black tea to green tea, or a green tea to herbal.
- **Week of Jan 18:** Make your afternoon cup herbal. Peppermint, rooibos, and hibiscus are good, and hibiscus iced with sparkling water is a great soda substitute.
- **Week of Jan 25:** Settle at whatever level feels good, such as one morning black tea.

## Avoiding headaches
- **Keep caffeine timing consistent.** Drink your caffeine at roughly the same times each day, and have the first cup in the morning, since withdrawal often hits then.
- **Stay hydrated.** Mild dehydration makes caffeine headaches worse, and sparkling water counts.
- **Back off if you get a headache.** Return to the previous step for a few extra days. A slower taper is still a win.
- **Expect sugar cravings around 3pm.** Four sodas is about 150 g of sugar a day. Have a snack ready, like fruit, nuts, or a granola bar.

## Quick check-in each Sunday
1. Did I hit this week's target? If so, move to the next step. If not, repeat the week.
2. Any headaches or crashes? If so, slow down.

Would you like a printable version or a simple tracker you can keep at your desk?

**Subject:** Request to move thesis defence to October 2027, and question about funding

---

Dear Professor Nowak,

I'm writing to ask whether we could move my thesis defence from June to October 2027, and to ask your advice on extending my funding past September.

As you know, we received the decision on [paper title] from [journal name]. The reviewers requested a major revision, including [briefly name the main request, e.g. "additional experiments on larger datasets" or "a redesigned ablation study"]. I've gone through the reports carefully, and I estimate that redoing the experiments properly will take about three months. I'd rather address the comments thoroughly than rush them, both for the paper's chances and because this work makes up [a core chapter / a substantial part] of the thesis.

Here is my proposed timeline:

- **December 2026 – February 2027:** Rerun and extend the experiments
- **March 2027:** Finalise the revised manuscript and response to reviewers, and resubmit
- **March – July 2027:** Write the remaining thesis chapters in parallel, incorporating the revised results
- **August 2027:** Submit the thesis to examiners
- **October 2027:** Defence

I did consider keeping the June date and presenting the paper as "under revision". However, I think the chapter would be much stronger with the new results included. A June defence would also mean writing the thesis and running the experiments at the same time on a very tight schedule. I'd value your view on this, though, if you think June is still realistic.

The main complication is funding. My current funding ends in September 2027, so the new schedule would leave a gap of at least [one to two] months before the defence, plus any time needed for corrections. Do you know of any options that could cover this period? For example, an extension from the current grant, a departmental or graduate school completion fund, or a teaching or research assistant position. If there are applications involved, I'd like to start on them early, since some deadlines may fall well before next summer.

Would you have time to discuss this in the next week or two? I'm happy to meet whenever suits you, and I can bring a more detailed plan for the revision.

Thank you very much for your time and support.

Best regards,
Ali

---

**Before sending:**

1. **Fill in the brackets.** Naming the paper and the reviewers' main request shows you've already worked out the scope of the revision.
2. **Check the revision deadline.** If the journal gave you a resubmission date, mention it (e.g. "the journal has asked for the revision by 15 March"). It makes your three-month estimate concrete.
3. **Check your university's rules first.** Look up:
   - How far in advance the thesis must go to examiners. I assumed about 6–8 weeks; adjust the August date if needed.
   - Whether moving the defence needs a formal request to the graduate school.
   - Whether there's a maximum registration period or "writing-up" status that affects fees or funding.
   
   If you already know of a specific fund, name it in the email. It shows initiative and makes her answer easier.
4. **Work out the funding gap.** If your defence is in October, you'll likely need funding until the end of October at minimum, and possibly longer for corrections. Give her a specific figure, like "October–November", rather than leaving it open.
5. **Keep the "considered June" paragraph or cut it.** It shows you've thought it through and leaves the decision with her, which supervisors usually appreciate. If you're certain June is unworkable, remove it to keep the email shorter.
6. **Send it soon.** It's mid-November, so asking now gives her time to reschedule and find funding. Many funding deadlines fall in the spring.

Let me know if you'd like a shorter version, a more formal tone, or a version to forward to your graduate school.

# Winter Revision Schedule: 24 December to 20 January

## How the plan is built

| **English** | Wed 20 Jan | Three full days (17th–19th) |

**Main decisions**

1. **Statistics gets about 45–50% of study time before the 13th**, roughly 47 hours. It is your hardest subject and your first exam.
2. **History has to be ready before the exams start.** You only get one afternoon for it between Economics and History, so it is studied steadily alongside Stats. The afternoon of the 15th is for final review only.
3. **Economics gets steady practice now and one full day on the 14th.**
4. **English is mostly left until 17–19 January.** Before then you only do a short daily habit so it doesn't go cold.
5. **The Osaka trip is a full break.** The plan expects some forgetting over the trip, so 4 January is a review day rather than a day for new material.

**Assumptions** (tell me if any are wrong and I'll adjust):
- 29 December and 3 January are travel days with no study.
- Exams are in the morning. If one is in the afternoon, you gain a few hours that morning.
- You have past papers or practice questions. If you don't, use textbook end-of-chapter questions or ask your teachers.

**Approximate total hours**

| Subject | Hours |
|---|---|
| Statistics | ~47 |
| Economics | ~25 |
| Japanese History | ~21 |
| English | ~19 (about 15 of them on 17–19 Jan) |

## Daily structure

| Block | Time | What it's for |
|---|---|---|

## Phase 1: Foundations (Thu 24 – Mon 28 December)

The goal is to find out exactly where you are weak and start fixing Statistics. You also make condensed notes for Economics and History so they are ready to review in January.

Then stop. |

---

## Osaka: Tue 29 December – Sun 3 January

**No study.** Rest properly, see family and enjoy New Year. A real break helps you work better on the 9-day run that follows. Some forgetting is normal and the plan allows for it. Try to keep a roughly normal sleep pattern so 4 January isn't a struggle.

The goal is to finish all Stats topics, then switch to timed past papers and an error log. Economics and History move from making notes to testing yourself.

**Daily English habit, 5–11 January:** spend 20 minutes a day on English, for example flashcards, one short reading, or one paragraph of timed writing. It isn't listed in the table. Do it whenever you have energy, such as after lunch.

Eat well and go to bed early. |

---

## Phase 3: Exam period (Wed 13 – Wed 20 January)

| Date | Plan |
|---|---|
| **Wed 13 Jan** · **STATISTICS EXAM** | Before the exam, look over your formula sheet for 15 minutes, no more. **Afterwards, don't go through answers with friends.** Rest for 2 hours, then do 1.5–2 h of light Econ review: flashcards and drawing diagrams from memory. |
| **Thu 14 Jan** · Econ day | **B1:** Econ Past Paper #2, timed. **B2:** mark it, fix weak topics, and redraw every diagram from memory. **B3:** 1 h of History flashcards and timeline review, so History is still fresh on the 15th. Go to bed early. |
| **Fri 15 Jan** · **ECONOMICS EXAM** | After lunch, do **3–3.5 h of History, testing yourself only.** Write the timeline from memory, rehearse your essay plans aloud, and go through your flashcards. Don't make new notes. Go to bed early. |
| **Sat 16 Jan** · **JAPANESE HISTORY EXAM** | After the exam, **take the rest of the day completely off.** You've done three exams in four days. |
| **Sun 17 Jan** · English day 1 | **B1:** review your notes on the core content, such as set texts, key quotations and themes, or grammar rules. **B2:** practise the skills the exam tests. **B3:** vocabulary and quotation flashcards. |
| **Mon 18 Jan** · English day 2 | **B1:** English Past Paper, timed. **B2:** mark it and fix weaknesses. **B3:** practise essay plans, or timed writing on one more question. |
| **Tue 19 Jan** · Day before English, finish by about 17:00 | Do light consolidation: flashcards, quotations, essay plans and one short timed piece of writing. Prepare your kit and go to bed early. |
| **Wed 20 Jan** · **ENGLISH EXAM** | You're finished. Celebrate. 🎉 |

---

## How to study each subject

**Statistics (most important)**
- **Do problems instead of re-reading notes.** In Stats, understanding comes from working questions yourself. Look at a worked example once, then cover it and do it yourself.
- **Keep the error log.** By 12 January it should be your most useful revision document, because it lists exactly what you get wrong and why.
- **Practise choosing the right method.** Many marks are lost by picking the wrong test or distribution. For each question type, ask yourself what tells you which method to use: the data type, the sample size, whether the population standard deviation is known, and how many groups there are.
- **Write out interpretations in full,** for example "At the 5% level, there is sufficient evidence to reject H₀…". These sentences often carry marks.
- Common topics to check against your syllabus: probability rules, binomial, Poisson and normal distributions, sampling distributions and the Central Limit Theorem, confidence intervals, hypothesis tests (z, t, χ²), correlation and regression.

**Economics**
- **Practise diagrams until you can draw them from memory.** You should be able to draw each one, label it correctly, and explain what each shift means.
- **Practise calculations** such as elasticity, multipliers and GDP or inflation measures, because they are reliable marks.
- For essays, use a structure: definition, then diagram, then explanation, then a real-world example, then evaluation.

**Japanese History**
- **The timeline is the backbone of your revision.** You should be able to write it from memory by 15 January.
- **Learn causes and consequences, not just dates.** Examiners reward explanations of *why* something happened and *what it changed*.
- Prepared **essay plans** let you answer most likely questions quickly in the exam.
- Flashcards work well for names, dates and terms. Little and often is better than long sessions.

**English**
- The 20-minute daily habit stops this subject going cold while you focus on the others.
- Use 17–19 January for **exam-skill practice** such as timed writing and past papers, more than for re-reading.

---

## If things don't go to plan

- **If Stats is going slower than planned:** take time from B3 on 5–11 January first. If you need more, use the Saturday 9th evening off. **Don't cut History below the planned time,** because there is no time later to catch up.
- **If Stats is going well:** move spare blocks to Economics, which has the next tightest timing.
- **If you get ill or lose a day:** move everything back by one day and skip the lowest-priority B3 block from the following days. Don't try to fit two days' work into one.
- **If an exam is in the afternoon:** use that morning for 1–1.5 h of light review of the formula sheet, flashcards or plans. Don't learn new material.
- **Christmas or New Year plans** can replace any B3 block in Phase 1 without much cost.

## General tips

- **Sleep matters.** Memory consolidates during sleep, so an extra hour of late-night study usually costs more than it gains, especially the night before an exam.
- Keep your phone in another room during blocks.
- Short daily exercise or walks help concentration.
- Before each exam, check the time, the room, and what you're allowed to bring in.

---

If you send me your **actual syllabus topics** for each subject, I can replace the generic "🔴 topic #1" slots with named topics in a sensible order. For Statistics, for example, that might be probability, then distributions, then sampling, then inference, then regression. Good luck! 頑張って!

| **Agent D** | M | L | L | M | E | 1 / 0 / 2 / 2 |
| **Agent E** | L | L | M | E | D | 1 / 1 / 1 / 2 |
| **Agent F** | L | M | E | D | M | 1 / 1 / 2 / 1 |
| **Agent G** | M | E | D | M | L | 1 / 1 / 2 / 1 |

**Daily check:**

| Day | Early (07–15) | Day (09–17) | Mid (11–19) | Late (14–22) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Mon | Marta, B | C | D, G | E, F |
| Tue | Marta, G | B | C, F | D, E |
| Wed | Marta, F | G | B, E | C, D |
| Thu | Marta, E | F | D, G | B, C |
| Fri | Marta, D | E | C, F | B, G |

## Hour-by-hour coverage (identical every day)

| Time | 07–09 | 09–11 | 11–14 | 14–15 | 15–17 | 17–19 | 19–22 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| People on desk | **2** | 3 | 5 | 7 | 5 | 4 | **2** |

- The minimum of 2 is never breached.
- 14:00–15:00 is when all shifts overlap. It's a natural slot for handover or a daily 10-minute team huddle.
- The thinnest windows are opening (07–09) and closing (19–22), with exactly 2 people each. No breaks should be scheduled in those windows.

## Rest-period check

The rotation always moves forward through the day (E → D → M → L), so no one ever finishes at 22:00 and starts at 07:00 the next morning.

- The tightest gap is Late into Day (22:00 → 09:00), which is exactly 11 hours. It never actually occurs this week.
- The other gaps are 12 hours or more, for example Mid into Early (19:00 → 07:00).

## Suggested break windows

Every break below is taken while at least 3 others are on the desk.

| Shift | Break window | People still on desk |
|---|---|---|
| E | 11:00–12:30 (stagger the two agents) | 4+ |
| D | 12:30–13:30 | 4 |
| M | 15:00–16:30 (stagger) | 4 |
| L | 17:00–18:45 (stagger, back by 19:00) | 3 |

## Fairness over multiple weeks

Marta is fixed on Earlies. The other six agents rotate patterns each week: next week, B takes C's row, C takes D's, and so on, with G taking B's.

- The patterns contain 2, 2, 2, 2, 1 and 1 Late shifts. Over a 6-week cycle, everyone works every pattern once, so everyone does exactly 10 Lates.
- Because there's a weekend gap, changing patterns between Friday and Monday never causes a rest-period problem.
- Marta works no Lates, which means the other six carry them. That's usually accepted for a fixed childcare constraint, but it's worth being open with the team about it.

## Sickness and holiday cover

The rota has built-in slack: 7 people per day when 4 is the strict minimum.

- **An Early agent is absent:** the Day agent (09–17) moves to 07:00–15:00.
- **A Late agent is absent:** one Mid agent (11–19) switches to 14:00–22:00. Check that they didn't work an Early that morning.
- **Holidays:** up to 2 people per day can be off and you still have at least 2 Earlies and 2 Lates. Approve leave so that no day has more than 2 off.
- **Marta can only cover Early shifts.** If she's off, the other Early agent is still there and the Day agent moves up to 07:00.

## Lean alternative (if agents aren't all full-time)

If you only want to staff what's required plus break cover, use 5 people per day:

- 2 × E (Marta + 1)
- 1 × M (11–19)
- 2 × L

| Time | 07–11 | 11–14 | 14–15 | 15–19 | 19–22 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| People on desk | 2 | 3 | 5 | 3 | 2 |

This needs 25 shifts a week. Marta does 5, and the other six do 3–4 each. It still meets the minimum and covers breaks, but there's almost no slack for sickness, so a single absence on a Late puts you at risk.

## Points to confirm

1. **Contracted hours:** are all 7 full-time? This decides between the main rota and the lean version.
2. **Demand pattern:** are mornings or evenings busier? I assumed a midday peak. If evenings are busier, you could swap the Day shift (09–17) for a second Mid or a 12:00–20:00 shift.
3. **Marta:** is a 15:00 finish fine, or would she prefer 08:00–16:00? Either works, but with 08:00–16:00 the other Early agent would be alone from 07:00 to 08:00, so you'd need a third Early agent.
4. **Breaks:** are they paid and included in the 8 hours, and what length is legally required where you are?

I can also make the lean version as a full grid, a 6-week rotation calendar, or a CSV/spreadsheet you can paste into your scheduling tool.

Q51-B.text:
# Your Farmhouse-to-Ennis Move Plan

**The facts this plan is built on:** 40 years of belongings, moving to a 2-bed bungalow in Ennis at the end of February, no attic or garage, and Declan's van for two weekends only.

**The two dates to lock in with Declan now:**
- **Weekend 1: Saturday 30 – Sunday 31 January 2027** (the clear-out)
- **Weekend 2: Saturday 27 – Sunday 28 February 2027** (the move)

If you hand over the farmhouse keys before 27 February, move Weekend 2 back to 20–21 February. Everything else stays the same.

---

## Part 1: How to decide what stays and what goes

### The one rule
**If it doesn't have a specific spot in the bungalow, it doesn't come.** There is no attic or garage to catch the "maybes," so every item you bring must have a named place, such as "the hall cupboard" or "under the spare bed."

### Before you sort anything (this week)
1. Get the bungalow's floor plan from the estate agent or measure it yourselves. Note the wall lengths, the window and radiator positions, and the size of each built-in wardrobe and cupboard.
2. Walk the farmhouse and choose the furniture for each bungalow room. Most of the farmhouse furniture will not come. The usual fit for a 2-bed bungalow is:
   - **Living room:** one sofa, two armchairs at most, one TV unit, one side table, and one bookcase
   - **Kitchen/dining:** a table and chairs for 4 to 6
   - **Main bedroom:** your bed, two bedside lockers, one chest of drawers, and a wardrobe only if there is no built-in one
   - **Second bedroom:** a double or sofa bed for visitors, plus one piece of storage furniture
3. Measure each chosen piece and check it fits, including doorways.

### Keep / Sell / Give / Bin: the decision for each item

| Ask yourself | If yes… |
|---|---|
| Do we use it at least once a year, and does it have a named spot in the bungalow? | **KEEP** |
| Does one of the family want it? | **GIVE TO FAMILY** (they collect by the deadline below) |
| Would someone pay more than €30 for it? | **SELL** |
| Is it clean, working and useful? | **GIVE TO CHARITY** |
| None of the above | **BIN / RECYCLE** |

### Limits for the hardest categories
- **Keepsakes:** one large lidded box each, plus one shared box. Whatever fits in the boxes comes, and nothing more.
- **Photos:** keep the albums that matter most. Scan or photograph the loose prints and slides, or pay a local photo shop to digitise them. Offer the originals to the family before discarding any.
- **Kitchen:** everyday dishes, glasses and cutlery for 6. Keep one set of good pots and the baking things you actually use. Duplicates go.
- **Linen:** two sets per bed and four towels each, plus one guest set.
- **Books:** whatever fits on the one bookcase you are taking.
- **Clothes:** what fits your built-in wardrobes and drawers. If you haven't worn it in two winters, it goes.
- **Tools and garden:** one small toolbox. A bungalow with no garage has no room for farm tools, mowers or workbench gear, so sell these.
- **Paperwork:** keep property, pension, medical, tax (last 6 years) and legal documents in one box file. Shred the rest.

### Where things go
- **Selling everyday items:** DoneDeal, Adverts.ie and Facebook Marketplace. Price to go, at about a third of the original cost, and buyers collect.
- **Antiques, old dressers, clocks and good furniture:** ask a local auctioneer for a valuation. Many do house-contents auctions and will take a whole lot at once, which saves you selling piece by piece.
- **Machinery, tools and outdoor items:** DoneDeal is the strongest market for these.
- **Charity:** St Vincent de Paul in Ennis takes furniture and household goods. Ring ahead, because some furniture needs to be collection-only and bookings can be weeks out. Clothes, books and bric-a-brac can go to any charity shop.
- **Rubbish and recycling:** your Clare County Council recycling centre. Check clarecoco.ie for hours and charges before Weekend 1. For a large final amount, a skip delivered to the farmhouse in February is often easier.

---

## Part 2: The timeline

### Now to 14 December: decide the big things
- Book both weekends with Declan.
- Get the floor plan and pick the furniture that's coming.
- Get the auctioneer out for anything that might have value.
- Book an SVP collection for late January if you have furniture to donate.
- Buy 40 sturdy boxes, tape, marker pens and coloured stickers in four colours: **Keep** (green), **Family** (blue), **Sell** (yellow), **Charity** (red).

### Christmas: family claim time
While the family is home, each person walks the house and puts blue stickers with their name on anything they want. **Their deadline is 31 January.** Anything not collected by then, or taken in Declan's van on Weekend 1, goes to sale or charity. Christmas is also a good time to go through the photos together.

### 4 January to 29 January: sort and sell
- **Do one room per week, starting with the least-used rooms:**
  - Week of 4 Jan: spare rooms
  - Week of 11 Jan: sheds and outbuildings
  - Week of 18 Jan: living and dining rooms
  - Week of 25 Jan: bedroom wardrobes and drawers
- **Do two hours a day, not whole days.** Sorting 40 years of belongings is tiring and emotional.
- **List all sell items by 15 January.** Selling takes weeks, and you want buyers collecting through January and February.
- **Stack charity and rubbish in one room or shed,** ready for Weekend 1.

### Weekend 1: Saturday 30 – Sunday 31 January (the clear-out)
**Saturday:**
- **Morning:** recycling centre run, with the heaviest rubbish first.
- **Afternoon:** charity runs (SVP and charity shops) for anything not collected.
- **Evening:** a second recycling run if needed.

**Sunday:**
- **Morning:** family items into the van for delivery to whoever claimed them.
- **Afternoon:** if you have the bungalow keys by then, take a first load of packed boxes you won't need before the move, such as books, spare linen, ornaments and the keepsake boxes. If you don't have the keys, Declan helps you dismantle and stack anything left for the auctioneer or buyers.

**The goal:** by Sunday night the farmhouse holds only what you're keeping and what's sold or awaiting collection.

### 1 February to 26 February: final stretch
- **Week of 1 Feb:** final sell-off. Anything still unsold by 14 February goes to charity or to the auctioneer's lot.
- **Week of 8 Feb:** pack everything non-essential. Label each box with the **bungalow room** it goes to, not the farmhouse room.
- **Week of 15 Feb:** order a skip or arrange a final clearance for leftovers. Redirect post through An Post, and transfer electricity, broadband and bin services to the Ennis address.
- **Week of 22 Feb:** pack the kitchen, leaving out the kettle, a few mugs and plates.
- **Friday 26 February:** take beds apart and pack one "first night" bag each, containing:
  - medication
  - phone chargers
  - toiletries
  - bedlinen for your bed
  - kettle, tea and mugs
  - toilet roll
  - a few tools for reassembling the bed

### Weekend 2: Saturday 27 – Sunday 28 February (the move)
**Saturday:**
- **Early start:** load the heavy furniture first (beds, wardrobe, chest of drawers, sofa, table), then fill the gaps with boxes.
- **Drive to Ennis:** unload the furniture straight into its correct room using your floor plan, and set up your bed first.
- **Afternoon:** second load of boxes.

**Sunday:**
- **Morning:** final load from the farmhouse.
- **Afternoon:** do a final walk-through of the farmhouse. Check the meters, take readings and photos, and lock up. Unpack the kitchen and bathroom in the bungalow first.

**Van check:** Before Weekend 1, ask Declan to look at your keep list and say honestly whether it fits in **two or three van loads**. If it won't, book a local removal firm to bring just the large furniture on 27 February, and use Declan's van for the boxes. Settle this by mid-January so you're not caught short on moving day.

---

## Part 3: Three things that will make the biggest difference
1. **Decide the furniture first.** Once you know which pieces are going, everything else gets easier.
2. **Set deadlines and stick to them.** "Family by 31 January, unsold by 14 February" stops things lingering until the move.
3. **Label boxes by bungalow room.** With no attic or garage to dump things in, every box needs to go straight where it belongs.

Good luck to you both in Ennis.

Q45-B.text:
# Family Dinner for 18: Thursday to Saturday Cooking Plan

I've planned around **serving dinner at 7:00pm Saturday with guests arriving at 6:00pm**. If your time is different, shift every Saturday time by the same amount.

The menu is **vegetarian**, and **everything except the paneer dish, the raita and the naan is vegan**. The three grandchildren get a full meal and you only need to keep three things separate.

## The Menu

| Dish | Vegan? | When it's cooked |
|---|---|---|
| Onion bhajis (starter) | ✅ Vegan | Fried Friday, re-crisped Saturday |
| Chana masala | ✅ Vegan (oil, no ghee) | Thursday |
| Tarka dal | ✅ Vegan (oil tadka) | Lentils Thursday, tadka Saturday |
| Paneer butter masala | ❌ Paneer, butter, cream | Sauce Thursday, finished Saturday |
| Roast aloo gobi | ✅ Vegan | Friday, reheated Saturday |
| Jeera rice | ✅ Vegan | Saturday only (see food safety) |
| Kachumber salad | ✅ Vegan | Saturday afternoon |
| Cucumber raita | ❌ Yoghurt | Saturday afternoon |
| Naan | ❌ Most contain milk | Shop-bought, warmed Saturday |
| Chapatis | ✅ Vegan (check label) | Shop-bought, for the vegans |
| Coconut cardamom kheer | ✅ Vegan | Friday, served cold |

## Shopping List (buy Thursday morning)

**Dry and tinned goods**
- 1 kg red lentils (masoor dal)
- 6 × 400g tins chickpeas
- 6 × 400g tins chopped tomatoes
- 1.8 kg basmati rice for the main meal, plus 200g for the kheer
- 500g gram flour (besan)
- 100g cashews
- 4 × 400ml tins full-fat coconut milk
- 1 litre oat milk
- 200g sugar
- 50g shelled pistachios
- 1 litre vegetable or sunflower oil for frying, plus extra for cooking
- 30 naan
- 12 chapatis labelled vegan. Plain chapatis are usually just flour, water and oil, but check, because many naan contain milk or yoghurt.

**Spices**
- Cumin seeds
- Ground cumin
- Ground coriander
- Turmeric
- Garam masala
- Kashmiri chilli powder
- Dried red chillies
- Green cardamom pods
- 2 tbsp kasuri methi (dried fenugreek)
- Amchur, or use lemon instead

**Fresh**
- 12 large onions
- 4 red onions
- 2 bulbs garlic
- 200g ginger
- 8 green chillies
- 4 large bunches coriander
- 2 large cauliflowers
- 1.5 kg potatoes
- 5 cucumbers
- 8 tomatoes
- 4 lemons

**Dairy (non-vegan dishes only)**
- 1.5 kg paneer
- 300ml double cream
- 75g butter
- 1 kg plain yoghurt

## THURSDAY: Shop, then make the three curry bases (about 3 hours of cooking)

**Afternoon**

- **2:00pm: Ginger-garlic paste.** Blitz 2 bulbs of peeled garlic and 200g ginger with 4 tbsp oil. Store it in a jar in the fridge. You'll use it all week.
- **2:30pm: Chop 7 onions.** You need 4 for the chana, 2 for the makhani sauce and 1 for the dal.

**3:00pm: Three rings going at once**

- **Ring 1: Chana masala (vegan)**
  1. Fry 4 chopped onions in 6 tbsp oil for 15 minutes until deep golden.
  2. Add 4 tbsp ginger-garlic paste and 2 chopped green chillies. Cook for 2 minutes.
  3. Add 2 tbsp ground coriander, 1 tbsp ground cumin, 1 tsp turmeric and 2 tsp chilli powder. Cook for 1 minute.
  4. Add 3 tins tomatoes and cook for 15 minutes until the oil separates.
  5. Add 6 drained tins of chickpeas, 500ml water and 2 tsp salt. Simmer for 25 minutes.
  6. Stir in 2 tsp garam masala.
- **Ring 2: Dal base (vegan)**
  1. Rinse 1 kg red lentils.
  2. Simmer them in 4 litres water with 1 chopped onion, 2 tsp turmeric and 1 tbsp salt for 30 minutes, stirring often, until soft.
  3. Whisk smooth.
  4. Stop here. The tadka goes on fresh on Saturday.
- **Ring 3: Makhani sauce base**
  1. Fry 2 chopped onions in 3 tbsp oil for 10 minutes.
  2. Add 3 tbsp ginger-garlic paste, 3 tins tomatoes, 100g cashews, 2 tsp chilli powder and 2 tsp salt. Simmer for 25 minutes.
  3. Blend it smooth.
  4. Don't add the butter, cream or paneer yet.

**5:00pm: Cool and fridge**

- Spread each pot into wide containers so they cool fast.
- Get them all into the fridge within 2 hours.
- Label them clearly: **"CHANA – VEGAN"**, **"DAL – VEGAN"**, **"MAKHANI – DAIRY"**.

## FRIDAY: Oven day and frying day (about 4 hours)

**Morning**

- **9:30am: Kheer (Ring 1, vegan)**
  1. Simmer 200g rinsed rice in 1 litre oat milk with 8 crushed cardamom pods for 25 minutes, stirring often.
  2. Add 4 tins coconut milk and 200g sugar. Simmer for 20 more minutes, stirring, until thick.
  3. Cool it, cover it and chill it. Keep the pistachios aside for Saturday.
- **10:00am: Aloo gobi prep**
  1. Cut 2 cauliflowers into florets and 1.5 kg potatoes into 3cm chunks.
  2. Toss everything with 8 tbsp oil, 2 tbsp ginger-garlic paste, 2 tsp turmeric, 2 tsp cumin seeds, 2 tsp ground coriander, 2 tsp chilli powder, 2 tsp amchur or the juice of 1 lemon, and 1 tbsp salt.
- **10:30am: Oven at 200°C, one tray at a time**
  - Tray 1 goes in at 10:30 and comes out at 11:05.
  - Tray 2 goes in at 11:05 and comes out at 11:40.
  - Tray 3 goes in at 11:40 and comes out at 12:15.
  - Each tray takes about 35 minutes. Turn the vegetables halfway.
  - Cool, combine everything into one large covered container and refrigerate.

**Afternoon**

- **1:00pm: Bhajis (Ring 2, vegan)**
  1. Thinly slice 5 large onions.
  2. Mix them with 500g gram flour, 2 tsp each of cumin seeds, turmeric and chilli powder, 2 chopped green chillies, 1 bunch chopped coriander and 2 tsp salt.
  3. Add about 300ml water, just enough to make it hold together.
  4. Deep-fry spoonfuls at 170°C, 8 at a time, for 5 to 6 minutes. That's about 7 batches, roughly 50 bhajis, taking about 45 minutes.
  5. Cool them on a rack, then fridge them in containers lined with kitchen paper.
- **3:00pm: Set up for Saturday**
  - Set the table.
  - Put out the serving dishes and serving spoons.
  - Stick labels on the dishes: vegan dishes in one colour, dairy dishes in another.
  - **Give each vegan dish its own spoon** so no paneer sauce gets carried over.

## SATURDAY: Assemble, reheat, serve

**Afternoon (calm, all cold prep)**

- **2:00pm: Kachumber (vegan)**
  - Dice 4 cucumbers, 8 tomatoes and 4 red onions.
  - Add 2 chopped green chillies and 1 bunch coriander.
  - Cover and chill. **Add the salt and the juice of 3 lemons only at 6:50pm** so it doesn't go watery.
- **2:30pm: Raita**
  - Mix 1 kg yoghurt with 1 grated, squeezed cucumber, 1 tsp roasted ground cumin and 1 tsp salt. Chill.
- **3:00pm: Prep the paneer**
  - Cut 1.5 kg paneer into 2cm cubes. Keep them covered in the fridge.
- **3:15pm: Prep for the dal tadka**
  - Slice 10 garlic cloves.
  - Measure 6 tbsp oil, 2 tsp cumin seeds and 6 dried red chillies into a small bowl.
- **3:30pm: Rest.** Get changed.
- **5:15pm: Soak the rice**
  - Rinse 1.8 kg basmati until the water runs clear.
  - Split it between 2 bowls and soak for 30 minutes.
  - Take the chana, dal and makhani out of the fridge.
- **5:45pm: Drain the rice. Preheat the oven to 200°C.**

**Final hour: oven and all 4 rings**

| Time | Oven (one tray) | Ring 1 | Ring 2 | Ring 3 | Ring 4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 5:55 | Bhajis tray 1 (10 min) | | | | |
| 6:00 | | **Rice pot A:** 1 tbsp cumin seeds in 2 tbsp oil, add 900g rice and 1.4 L boiling water with 2 tsp salt, then boil | **Rice pot B:** same as pot A | | |
| 6:05 | Bhajis tray 2 (10 min) | Lid on, lowest heat for 12 min | Lid on, lowest heat for 12 min | | |
| 6:15 | Serve bhajis as the starter. Turn the oven down to 190°C. | | | **Dal:** splash of water, stir and bring to a simmer | **Chana:** splash of water, stir and bring to a simmer |
| 6:17 | | Off the heat, lid on, rest it on the side | Off the heat, lid on, rest it on the side | | |
| 6:20 | **Aloo gobi**, all in one deep tray, foil on (30 min) | **Makhani sauce:** reheat, stirring | | Simmering, stir often | Simmering, stir often |
| 6:40 | | Add 75g butter, 300ml cream, 2 tbsp kasuri methi (crushed) and the paneer. Simmer for 5 min. | **Tadka pan:** oil, cumin, garlic and chillies until the garlic turns golden. Pour onto the dal. | Lowest heat | Lowest heat |
| 6:50 | Aloo gobi out. Naan and chapatis go in as **two separate foil parcels** (8 min). | Off | Off | Off | Off |
| 6:50 | Dress the kachumber. Take out the kheer and scatter the pistachios on top. | | | | |
| **7:00** | **Serve** | | | | |

You never use more than 4 rings at once, because the rice is off the heat before the makhani and tadka start. The oven only ever holds one tray. Cooked rice stays hot with the lid on for well over 40 minutes. Fluff it with a fork just before serving.

## Keeping it safely vegan and safe to eat

- **No ghee anywhere.** All tadkas and frying use oil. Don't finish the dal with butter. If others want butter, put a dish of it on the table.
- **Keep the naan and chapatis in separate foil parcels.** Put the chapatis next to the vegan dishes.
- **Use separate serving spoons** for the vegan dishes, and serve the vegan grandchildren first if you can.
- **The rice is cooked only on Saturday.** Cooked rice kept for days is a known food-poisoning risk. The curries are fine for 2 days in the fridge, as long as they're cooled quickly and **reheated once, until piping hot all the way through**.
- **Leftovers:** fridge them within 1 hour of the meal ending, and eat them within 2 days.
